Research on top quarks at hadron colliders is pivotal in not only understanding the fundamental composition of matter but also in detecting signs of physical processes that go beyond the realm of standard models. The LHC's experiments on top quark production paired with new physics interactions have the potential to reveal a wide range of new phenomena. In this research paper, we develop an analytical framework to explore how the lenticular shape of the top quark production forward aperture, combined with new physics interactions, can provide insights into the behavior of new particles and their properties. The proposed model considers various new particles with different spin configurations and decay patterns. The relationships between these new particles and top quarks are studied using event selections based on decay patterns and forward cutting parameters. The findings are illustrated by researching the behavior of vector boson, scalar, and fermion mediators in relation to top quark production. The advantage of using vector mediators is that they can be distinguished from scalar mediators due to their capability to modify cross sections and modify memory effects. Additionally, our research shows that vector mediators have the potential to be probed at higher energies. The findings are further reinforced by simulations of event rates and contour plots.

This document establishes the fundamental elements for virtual organizations, requirement refinement, abstractions of models, and concrete instantiations. The document also examines Virtual Organizations within these contexts in detail.

Classic experience replay (ARL) has been a cornerstone of successful Reinforcement Learning, yet its assumption that past information remains static no longer holds in environments with dynamic changes, leading to heavily degraded performance. To mitigate this, researchers have developed specialized policies and architectures to process temporal changes, but these solutions often come with drawbacks such as increased complexity and resource demands. To address this limitation more effectively, our proposed approach involves reimagining the standard time parameter $\tau$ in experience replay as a predictive learning task. To facilitate seamless retrieval and labeling of this new 'replay time', our method utilizes temporal convolutional networks (TCNs) as encoder-decoder architecture, allowing the replay data to be predicted and decoded from the replay memory. As a result, the proposed approach exhibits remarkable efficiency when tested on the Robust RL benchmark and achieves superior performance while significantly reducing parameter count and memory usage compared to existing methods.

Two new strategies have been proposed to apply the supersymmetry method from Gaussian matrices to broader rotation-invariant matrices. Specifically, the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization formula have emerged as viable approaches. By showing the equivalence of these strategies, we aim to demonstrate their usefulness in broader applications, including new findings on the spectral statistics of certain Hermitian matrix classes that include the chiral GUE, GUC, GOE, and GSOB ensembles.

This paper addresses challenges in the spatiotemporal predictive learning domain, where information is given as a sequence of partial grids, spanning across space and time. Through application examples, we demonstrate how the 3D CNN-based solver in ST-PL presents difficulties, particularly in terms of memory usage and the z-axis resolution. To overcome these challenges, we introduce a two-stage solver, combining depth-wise 2D CNN and bidirectional RNN architectures. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach on three benchmark datasets: MNIST video, 3D sphères, and Iso864, where it rivals or surpasses the three existing benchmarks in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

This research focuses on bridging the gap between functional language memory management techniques and C-style allocation and allocation-free programming techniques. Traditionally, functional languages utilize reference counting to manage memory. In contrast, we explore an alternative approach that allows for explicit memory allocation in a manner reminiscent of C's memory management style, within the OCaml framework. The proposed solution leverages OCaml values' metadata, enabling a more flexible and practical memory management system. The safety of the system is established through a type system with a formal proof of type safety. The effectiveness of the system is demonstrated through several case studies that showcase its capabilities.

Theoretical particle physics predicts the existence of heavy neutral leptons arising from extended Standard Models,  which may contribute to key physical processes such as neutron decay, mass generation, and dark matter.  These particles, also referred to as sterile neutrinos, can be detected in searches involving the production of single or few leptons alongside missing energy.  A new search strategy at the Large Hadron Collider involves the examination of incorporated hadronic activity to explore the presence of heavy neutral lepton states.  To accomplish this, all analytical data collected by the CMS experiment via the Higgs boson via vector boson fusion at 13 TeV has been assessed.  In the investigated mass range of 28 to 500 GeV, no significant sign of heavy neutral leptons was found,  resulting in the establishment of new bounds on their cross-sectional occurrence.

Permutation decoding has become a popular approach to enhancing polar codes' performance while minimizing decoding complexity by utilizing specific, low-overhead decoders. Nevertheless, existing research has not thoroughly examined the most effective permutations for optimal performance. We propose a new method, permutation encoding, to determine the optimal permutations that facilitate the highest achievable performance in permutation decoding. Our results demonstrate significant, up to 0.25 dB, throughput enhancements over prior results, thereby validating the efficacy of permutation encoding. We further investigate the effects of various permutation properties and present multiple speculative possibilities, with one being successfully verified through analysis. Our results also reveal that certain permutations of 6 and 7 polar code ensemble codes outperform traditional iterative decoding methods, specifically BFOS, under specific conditions. Our work aims to provide a comprehensive framework for researchers to explore and advance the performance potential of permutation decoding methods.

To achieve precise photometry, astronomers need to create well-calibrated images by combining, or 'linear coadding', multiple images of the same area. However, to produce consistent, high-quality images through linear coaddition, a certain condition must be fulfilled: the point-source profiles, or point-spread functions (PSFs), across all images must be consistent. In this condition's absence, it is crucial to identify which pixels are affected by the coaddition's linearity violations. Our research reveals that such cases are not as uncommon as might be expected. Through analyzing various coadditions from the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE), we found that about 10% of them had inaccurate PSF adjustments. Consequently, about 10% of the coadditions contained star images with distorted shapes due to these inaccuracies, which could be detected by comparing their observed and expected distortions. Our study also discovered that these inaccuracies are more prevalent in smaller-sized stars, smaller seeing conditions, and shorter coadditions. Moreover, about 10% of these distortions were found to be uncorrectable through linear coaddition's limitations. These inaccuracies pose a significant issue for scientific research utilizing the WISE catalog, as they can introduce biased measurements of WISE source properties.

Our work builds on established thermodynamic principles to analyze the fracture process in materials, focusing on the evolution of dislocations as observed in experiments. Through this theoretical framework, fracture is viewed as a competition between dislocations moving along the crack and transitioning into the crystal bulk, both of which are governed by thermodynamic factors and dislocation densities in the crack. Notably, dislocations that form during deformation are considered mobile, allowing us to make predictions about fracture toughness that are consistent with experimental observations, including its dependence on strain rate and grain size. The approach highlights areas for further research, such as fracture toughness's potential correlation with dislocation density and thermodynamic characteristics of crystal boundaries.

The relationship between Gaussian free fields and a variety of stochastic processes such as the Dyson model, Brownian motion on Lie groups and the Schur algebra has been explored. A crucial property is the diagonalization of the free field via a direct sum over stochastic processes that belong to the diagonalization torus. Additionally, it's demonstrated that stochastic integrals involving the diagonalization process yield Schur algebra and Lie group / algebra elements. Specifically, certain process functionals correspond to invariant polynomials, while others translate to Lie group factorizations. Furthermore, the involution property of Schur algebra elements can be determined by the time-reversal behavior of these functionals. As an example, it's established that certain process functionals are linked to branching Schur algebra elements that match Young tableaux.

In this research, we address the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in multi-dimensional space with smooth periodic initial conditions and obtain analytical estimates of the solution's maximum norm in space and time-dependent norms. These solution bounds exhibit both time and period dependencies that are adjustable.

The verification problem for quantum computation is crucial in quantum information science, where a quantum server processes and transmits data, but has a classical client that doesn't trust the results, especially when involving multiple users. Our study reveals a key breakthrough in the classical verification problem for quantum computation, where we develop a single-server protocol using a quantum strategy and quantum channel, reducing round complexity to polynomial in the size of the input. Our protocol leverages a new state compression technique, using a quantum strategy compressor, and our results confirm the optimality of server speed, given the limitations of the quantum channel. Our classical verification protocol outperforms previous approaches, using a new speed limit and a quantum channel size proportional to the size of the input, and we show that a previous open problem is resolved, with a single-server verification protocol using a new quantum channel and state compression technique. Our results can be applied to the classical verification of quantum computation, where we optimize existing approaches and show that a single-server verification protocol using a quantum strategy and quantum channel is possible, with speed determined by a new quantum channel size. Our proof technique has further implications, where we show that a new lower bound applies to all possible classical verification protocols, even without round constraints.

A blockchain system enables secure communication among parties with conflicting interests through a trustworthy ledger with immutable records. The unique properties of blockchain, offering security, trust, and transparency, have made it a prime candidate for the development of trust-infused IoT, known as the IoT, on a large scale. The emergence of blockchain-based IoT, named Blockchain-IoT, is still in its early stages of development. This chapter seeks to shed light on the development of Blockchain-IoT by exploring the benefits and obstacles involved. It provides an in-depth analysis of the underlying architecture of Blockchain-IoT and the various blockchain frameworks that have been adopted. It also highlights the key research areas that are critical to fully actualize the potential of Blockchain-IoT.

Generating cell shapes from images is a complex process that's been approached in various ways. Signatures of signed distance functions (SDFs) have been shown to be advantageous over the traditional methods of voxel-based representations and polygon meshes. SDFs offer the benefits of implicit representation, high modeling precision, and efficient manipulation capabilities. Our proposed method involves using a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) to generate cell shapes, allowing for the direct encoding of complex geometries. The method's key aspect is the training process, where the SMLM task is used to teach the network to predict cell shapes. Our experiment has demonstrated that this approach can accurately reconstruct cell shapes and simulate shape changes in response to external stimuli.

Blind, low-vision, and other print-disabled individuals still struggle with printed documents. Our focus lies on addressing a particular issue: providing access to documents in both linear and two-dimensional formats. Most braille readers and screen readers lack the ability to preserve the original layout of documents, often forcing users to make difficult decisions between enjoying the benefits of linear consumption or maintaining two-dimensional information structure. This paper outlines our proposed solution and ongoing development of a high-level API, referred to as Laidout, which facilitates users in choosing between linear and two-dimensional representations of documents. Our system, referred to as Laidout+, leverages L API and a desktop braille display to deliver document content in an interactive SPOT ontology to braille displays. Our research involved user testing conducted on documents in both linear and two-dimensional formats with ten braille readers to gather feedback on the system's performance, often revealing that participants highly valued the system's interactivity and flexibility. Our research demonstrates that braille displays can effectively present interactive SPOT ontologies to braille readers in an interactive and customizable way.

While BERT excels at modeling bidirectional contexts through denoising autoencoding, its reliance on input masking overlooks positional dependencies, leading to inconsistent pretraining objectives and limited modeling capabilities. This has motivated the development of XLNet, an enhanced pretext pretraining approach based on masked autoregressive models. Building on successful applications of masked autoregressive transformers in modeling complex sequences, the XLNet architecture utilizes input masking to preserve autoregression while extending the context window from 512/1024 tokens in BERT to 512/2048 tokens in XLNet. Experimental evaluations across six benchmark tasks demonstrate that XLN extends input masking to preserve autoregression while extending context in BXT surpasses BERT consistently in natural language inference, core natural language processing, and word problem-solving evaluations, with margins reaching up to 10.0 points in optimized settings for SQuAD. Pretrained models and associated code can be accessed at https://github.com/zhaoyw95/XLNet.

We have developed synthetic transmission spectra for TRAPPIST-1's planetary system and planet-dwarf system analogs, focusing on how planetary water features are perceived by TRAPPI-1's observatory. We've integrated a line formation code with the Stellar Activity and Planetary Transit Simulator to analyze water signatures in various scenarios of stellar activity and planetary transit. Our approach allows us to simulate trace methane lines to study the combined effects of planetary atmospheric absorption and stellar activity on observed spectra. We've found that stellar activity can mimic planetary signatures and create artifacts in observed spectra. Specifically, we've found that the Ca II H&K emission line in neutral calcium is particularly sensitive to temperature changes and can be a significant factor in TRAPPI-1's spectrum during planetary transits. Our research highlights the need for careful consideration of stellar activity when analyzing transmission spectra of low-mass stars hosting multiple planets.

We will explicitly construct conformal metrics with constant curvature on Riemann surfaces featuring singularities using ODE derived from a type of meromorphic 1-forms. This approach will have an application in classifying a type of metric with constant curvature on the 2-sphere, specifically those with two conical singularities, which is analogous to a theorem initially established by Troyanov.

Research is conducted to study the movement of the centipede *Lithobacheus forficatus* at the air-water interface. This species of centipede, known to travel along water surfaces using leg movements, carries out experiments to measure the duration of its travel, the speeds at various sizes, the patterns of its movement, and the impact of different factors. Several experiments show that the speeds increase as the size of the centipede increases, but the patterns and frequency of its movement vary only slightly. Moreover, the speeds increase when water surface tension is present as opposed to clean water, while frequency and patterns remain relatively constant. Additionally, the findings indicate that the patterns of movement are not influenced by the direction of travel or the position of the centipede on its body, yet travel times increase in more viscous water, lower surface tension water, and water with higher density. A theoretical model is also developed to analyze these movements, supporting the idea that the direction of movement is primarily determined by the centroid of force application, while the patterns and frequency are largely independent. This theoretical understanding also helps to clarify why small creatures, such as insects, struggle to replicate these movements.

The ultimate goal of this study is to enhance the accuracy of warning systems for tsunami-related disasters by utilizing dispersive models that can accurately capture short-wavelength phenomena used in tsunami simulation. To achieve this, a rigorous mathematical analysis is presented for a newly developed, fully integrated two-phase model that seamlessly combines the effects of surface waves and sediment displacement across all depth levels. This novel model effectively encapsulates the complex interactions typically associated with the dispersion of waves and sediment displacement. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that the proposed model naturally reduces to the widely used, commonly-used two-phase model in the case of long-wavelength phenomena, thus encapsulating the well-established models in the existing scientific literature.

Recent research suggests that the cosmic star formation rate density at z~6-7 is lower than previously thought, potentially indicating a large number of under-observed HST-dark galaxies. To shed light on these elusive galaxies, we conducted a deep observation at 870 micrometers using the Submillimeter Array towards a bright BLA050 galaxy at z=6.6. Our findings reveal no substantial submillimeter emission from the galaxy, and we discovered a brighter source, and radio emission at 1.49 GHz from a nearby blazar, BLTG050, at z=6.58. Our non-detection of a BLA050 detection at submillimeter wavelengths and the detection of a nearby blazar, suggest that the area is devoid of under-observed HST-dark galaxies at this redshift, and the radio emission at 1.49 GHz is dominated by a highly variable blazar, rather than thermal emission from star-forming galaxies.

By incorporating two topological terms into the Einstein-Hilbert action, we have modified the equations of motion in seven-dimensional gravity. Subsequently, in conjunction with a Schwarzschild-like metric and an anisotropic but spherically symmetric spatial metric, we have derived and analyzed the properties of static, spherically-symmetric black holes. These black holes can exhibit either AdS or dS spacetimes, depending on a cosmological constant. Furthermore, through numerical integration, we have generated the metric functions and timelike conformal diagrams for various AdS black holes. Our results also include AdS black hole thermodynamics, which incorporates the influence of the added topological terms.

In a narrow channel, we examine particles in a two-dimensional system that reach a stable state when their density is high, and their movement is limited by the channel's width. Through time-based analysis of the channel's structure, we gain insight into the characteristics of these stable configurations, which vary depending on the channel's width and the particles' relative sizes. Additionally, we use the calculated structures to investigate how these stable configurations change over time, and how the scaling laws of key properties vary with channel width across different ranges宽广.

When mechanical stress is applied to disordered materials, the material not only shrinks or changes shape but also undergoes a unique, irregular transformation. This unique behavior is known as nonaffine deformation and is a defining characteristic of such materials. Understanding this phenomenon is crucial for controlling the material's mechanical properties, but it poses significant challenges due to experimental and theoretical limitations. Our research utilizes advanced computational techniques, specifically simulations and advanced modeling of materials such as 2D colloidal suspensions, to investigate this concept in detail. Our findings reveal that this unique behavior arises from the material's response to localized changes rather than a general one, which challenges the conventional understanding of disordered materials and highlights the potential of advanced modeling techniques, such as machine learning methods, to gain deeper insights into these complex systems.

This research investigates a population model, incorporating various species interacting with a contaminant environment, where the psychological effects of adult organisms coexist with environmental contaminants. To model this scenario, we utilize a system of two first-order nonlinear differential equations using an exponential kernel. Our findings ensure the existence and uniqueness of solutions for these systems across multiple initial conditions. To model the existence of global solutions, we apply the Banach contraction principle. Furthermore, we utilize an energy method for the unconditioned stability of the zero solution's asymptotic stability.

The researchers achieve decidability for an infinitely large group of axiomatic extensions to the Full Lambek logic, specifically those with certain weakening and contraction properties. This achievement builds on a previous result regarding the contraction counterparts of these extensions, while the relevant logic they generalize from does not allow weakening. Notably, the proof of decidability involves the development of a more complex and generalized version of the well-known Fitch model. This new model can be seen as a natural extension of the standard Fitch model. In the process, the team also addresses a long-standing question regarding interpolation property in Full Lambek logic variants that are axiomatized by the left and right versions of the absorption principle. They achieve this by employing a new method for constructing a new class of relational models that allow for a more precise and nuanced representation of these variants. This new method relies on a specific type of ordered algebraic structure that allows for an infinite product of these relational models to possess certain desired properties, including the preservation of the subformula property. This new method not only provides a new class of extensions to the Full Lambek logic but also allows for the generalization of previously established results regarding the absorption principle and its related properties.

Hierarchical taxonomies have become the foundation of many machine learning applications, yet traditional learning methods cannot directly apply to them, necessitating representation learning. Current focus is on learning tags within Euclidean space, whereas researchers are exploring alternatives like geometric spaces with distinct curvature properties, including hyperbolic space, which better captures the hierarchical structure of taxonomies through its negative curvature. By leveraging hyperbolic space's properties, researchers can assign lower distances to closely related items, offering potential benefits for various machine learning tasks. This study investigates machine translation tasks within hierarchically structured domain-specific vocabularies, replacing the standard English-German Gutenberg corpus with the MPII's MultiDomainVocab corpus covering German versions of diverse German technical and scientific vocabularies from the industrial setting. By adapting the GloVe model to account for domain transfer and domain-invariant word embeddings, the study examines their respective translation capabilities.

A comprehensive analysis has been conducted to investigate the dipole and quadrupole properties of small molecules containing up to four atoms. Our study builds on a previously developed approach to assess the reliability of these properties by comparing them across different levels of theory. Initially, we examined 12 molecules with significant intermolecular interactions, focusing on those with large dipole moments when aligned along their molecular axes. These include molecules driven by hydrogen bonding, bonding, van der Waals forces, and a combination of hydrogen bonding and electrostatic interactions. Our investigation also encompassed molecules featuring hydrogen bonding networks. Our findings reveal that accurately representing these interactions, particularly hydrogen bonding and electrostatics, necessitates a precise description of long-range electrostatics and electrostatic multipoles. Additionally, we explored molecules with notable hydrogen bonding networks. Our results for water clusters indicate that accurately modeling such structures requires a precise description of electrostatic multipoles. Finally, we studied molecular pairs exhibiting hydrogen bonding in different orientations. Our comparison of interaction dipole contributions indicates that accurately describing these non-equilibrium structures relies heavily on accurately oriented intermolecular electrostatic multipoles.

The focus of this study is on addressing the issues of impracticality, uncertainties, and inconsistencies in decision-making within industry, particularly in scenarios with delayed shipments and inaccurate budget projections. The proposed approach incorporates fuzzy arithmetic and its operators to handle and process imperfect data, offering a novel framework for handling industrial uncertainties. This framework will demonstrate its applicability and effectiveness through a case study of a company's decision-making process, where comparisons are made with other methods that fail to effectively tackle the problems of imperfect data. The proposed method's superiority is highlighted through its success in a real-world company's decision-making application.

Cyber-Physical Systems require robust resilience properties to withstand disruptions, yet a standardized approach remains underdeveloped. This paper utilizes established first-order logic to create a framework for formulating and examining resilience in CPS. The CPS model incorporates physical components, constraints, and cyber controls, with external events modeled as arbitrary first-order formulas influencing system dynamics. To measure resilience, a logic-based cost function is introduced, assigning penalties to violations and external intrusions. The CPS's resilience is expressed through customized resilience formulas that combine temporal logic and logic without a boolean, enabling the evaluation of resilience via novel, first-order based algorithms that leverage preimage computation and temporal reasoning. The result is an innovative and unified method that unites first-order logic with temporal logic and model checking to assess the system's resistance and overall resilience.

One of the most pressing mysteries in modern physics is the nature of dark matter. Although it's certain that dark matter exists, its constituent particles remain unknown. Various theories have been put forth, however, none of them have been definitively confirmed. One of the most intriguing candidates is feebly interacting dark matter, which can be detected through experiments on Earth. Recent findings by electron scattering off nucleons have been interpreted as a possible sign of axion-like particles, although other possibilities such as the dark photon, Z boson, or scalar particles should also be taken into account. This analysis considers these other candidates in relation to the current experiments.

Consider a complete, non-compact Riemannian manifold M with dimension m, equipped with the metric g, whose Bakry-\'{E}mery Ricci curvature is bounded below by zero. We derive a localized version of Hamilton's gradient estimate for the solutions to a nonlinear diffusion equation, which has a nonlinear term given by a convex, C^2 function u: R^m -> R. Consequently, we obtain a global version of such an estimate, as well as Log-Sobolev and Sobolev inequalities when additional non-negative concave entropy conditions are met.

Radio sources observed at 5 GHz with varying angular sizes were analyzed using the WMAP world map to account for the polarization angle influence of the Galactic plane. The polarization characteristics of these radio sources were determined from the residual polarization after subtracting the foreground emission. The study found that the median fractional polarization of the sources inversely correlates with angular size only for sources smaller than 5 inches, indicating that polarization properties cannot be reliably extrapolated from sources larger than 8 inches. Furthermore, the study discovered that approximately 30% of the sources exhibit significant polarization angles or fractions. Notably, the high-polarization fractions were primarily found in sources with smaller angular sizes less than 2.5 inches, indicating that these sources possess intrinsic polarization properties greater than 10%.

Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) are a type of mathematical model, defined within the framework of Markov chains, that involve both hidden and observable random variables, denoted as $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$, respectively. HMMs are typically utilized in scenarios where there is a one-to-one correspondence between the state space of $\mathbf{X}$ and the outcome space of $\mathbf{Y}$. However, there are practical applications, particularly in bioinformatics, where extending HMMs to accommodate multiple observable random variables, or 'cospinors', necessitates the development of novel inference methods. This paper addresses the limitations of existing approximate inference methods in handling large high-dimensional outcome spaces and introduces an exact method based on a recursive dynamic programming algorithm that efficiently calculates the joint, conditional, and marginal probabilities associated with the variables at each level of the model. The presented method also enables the calculation of optimal state or outcome sequences through a dynamic programming-based backtracking process. We illustrate the utility of this approach by applying it to the identification of transcription factor binding sites within DNA sequences.

We develop a class of stochastic advection problems to investigate turbulent transport properties, where the flow field statistics are represented as a continuous time Markov process. This representation accurately captures turbulence's essence, characterized by the shift from one coherent structure to another within the fluid. Our model's theoretical framework draws from the well-established theory of random processes and functional analysis. Within this framework, we derive equations for the turbulent transport operator and a corresponding spectral density function. This approach enables the computation of various statistical properties, including the turbulent diffusivity, without needing direct numerical simulations.

We maintain that many 'good' fits to elastic scattering data are unwarranted,
lacking a firm understanding of the underlying physics. We propose a novel
methodology to assess the efficacy of folding models for nuclear elastic
scattering and apply it to the specific case of $^{124}$Xe+$^{40}$Ca systems.
By calculating individual nucleon-nucleon interaction matrix elements between
the constituent nuclei, we calculate separate potential components for
these nucleons within the $^{124}$Xe+$^{40}$Ca system. These components are
then input into a three-dimensional macroscopic-microscopic folding model and
input into a time-dependent variational principle. Comparing cross sections
from the model with experimental data allows us to gain insight into the
strength of the density-dependent effective interaction relative to free
nucleon-nucleon interactions.

This paper examines the electromagnetic radiation behavior within a thin semiconductor slab when positioned between two ideal conductive plates, applying quantum statistical mechanics to predict its macroscopic properties under equilibrium conditions. Through this analysis, a quantum radiation model emerges that exhibits striking similarities to the 2D Cassey-Schulhof model in low-temperature environments. The model's thermodynamic characteristics show that, contrary to expectations for gases, the internal energy and pressure drop as temperature decreases, ultimately suggesting that low-temperature electromagnetic radiation behaves more like a photon-based condensate than a traditional gas.

Protecting users of location-based services with significant privacy requirements is extremely difficult when multiple locations are shared within a short time frame due to locations being inferred from previous visits. Existing privacy protection schemes often fall short in addressing this challenge, as they either obscure the origin location's privacy or interrupt the service by introducing unnecessary delays. This paper introduces an innovative, real-time mechanism for the confidential reporting of origin-and destination locations, without compromising accuracy or introducing delays. Our mechanism's primary innovation lies in automatically generating plausible locations based on the destination location, which are then reported to the service simultaneously with the true origin location. We extensively evaluate the effectiveness of our mechanism by utilizing real-world data to measure the quality of the synthetic origins and utilize an attack model to simulate how well it protects the destination location. Our results indicate that our mechanism outperforms existing schemes in virtually all scenarios.

A reliable place recognition system that functions effectively in areas with limited or no GPS data is essential for autonomous driving. The state-of-the-art DL-based systems, however, often rely heavily on access to real-time sensory data from the environment. The ability to using pre-extracted and stored scene features, in addition to the current features, would greatly enhance the performance of the system, but current SIFT-based methods fail to effectively use the former. We propose a new architecture that effectively integrates pre-extracted scene cues with the current scene information. Our approach, called AML-Net, is a lightweight ConvNet architecture that can classify and align two image pairs by utilizing both SIFT cues and deep features. By decoupling the tasks of place recognition and localization, and framing the latter as a sequence classification problem, our model reduces computational complexity and data storage requirements. Our experiments using carlog datasets show that combining scene cues with the archetypal image results in superior performance compared to using only the scene features.

Research on resting-state functional brain connectivity using fMRI reveals how brain regions interact across varying frequencies. Understanding brain connectivity across different groups is crucial, particularly in comparing patients and controls or identifying abnormal connectivity in patients. However, most studies on connectivity rely on single-site samples, which can limit the generalizability of results and ignore the variation in brain connectivity that can occur across different sites. By comparing multilevel models with and without accounting for site differences, our study demonstrates the significant impact of site effects on statistical testing, with multisite studies offering increased detection power but potentially giving rise to false positives due to confounding. Overall, our research emphasizes the necessity of considering site effects in connectivity studies and the benefit of integrating multisite data. By applying ICA and correlation methods to a publicly available dataset of over 1,000 individuals undergoing MRI scans, our study reveals substantial site effects on brain connectivity across various groups, with notable site differences observed in both intra- and inter-regional correlations. By pooling multisite data, our study found a significant boost in detection power and a more accurate estimation of connectivity relationships. Ultimately, our multisite comparison highlights the importance of accounting for site effects and the value of integrating multisite data to fully understand brain connectivity relationships.

In a single-hop beeping network, stations interact via one-bit messages. We explore the capabilities and limitations of distributed algorithms for determining unique station counts and individual IDs under strict time constraints. We develop an efficient algorithm operating within a time frame of $O(\sqrt{n\log n})$, but also establish a hard limit at $8\sqrt{n}$. Furthermore, even with relaxed timing, we found an optimal efficient upper bound of $\min\left\{\frac{32}{5}n\log n,\ 32n\right\}$ and an insurmountable lower bound of $\min\left\{\frac{4}{5}n\log n,\ \frac{4}{5}n\right\}$. The key innovation involves novel arithmetic operations over beeping signals that facilitate efficient distributed algorithms.

Creating code-mixed language embeddings poses a significant challenge, primarily due to language drift resulting in shorter word lengths on average. To address this issue, we introduce GL2-Vec, a universal embedding model tailored specifically for code-mixed texts. Unlike existing word embeddings that often struggle to capture meaningful vector representations of code-mixed language, GL2-Vec offers a standardized approach suitable for multiple code-mixed languages. The model combines grade-based vectorization and vector aggregation techniques to encode language-specific and graph-based semantic information present in mixed scripts. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of GL2-Vec in tasks such as classification and information retrieval in code-mixed texts. The GL2-Vec library, comprising data models for code-mixed texts in multiple languages, is now publicly available on GitHub.

Using a combination of density functional theory calculations and the Eliashberg theory, we investigated how the superconducting properties of H3S change in response to varying levels of pressure. Our results reveal that within a certain pressure range of 150 to 240 GPa, H3S exhibits a non-monotonic superconducting transition temperature curve. This non-monotonic behavior stems from the fact that the density of states at the Fermi level, which contributes to the electron-phonon coupling constant $\lambda$ and the superconducting transition temperature $T_c$, varies differently in response to these varying levels of pressure, as confirmed by our calculations using three distinct theoretical approaches. This discrepancy highlights the significance of accurately determining the zero point motion in molecular dynamics simulations to achieve precise predictions of the superconducting properties at high pressures.

This paper outlines a reliable and resilient motion planning solution that successfully integrates real-time map updates and network-based prey position information in the presence of dynamic and unpredictable obstacles. The proposed method consists of a global planner that utilizes network-based map data, along with an local planner that relies on pre-mapped terrain. A specialized communication module ensures that timely and accurate network updates are utilized in real time. By combining these components, robot navigation is optimized to combine the advantages of both map-based and terrain-based planning. The solution has been successfully tested through simulation and experimental validation.

This paper presents a visual relocalization technique utilizing 3D surfel maps and deep learning. A contrastive learning approach is employed to develop view embedding networks, enabling the determination of current location through the aggregation of feature similarities with existing view embeddings within a map. The integration of geometric reasoning into the training process helps mitigate issues of scale and geometric distortions. Notably, the trifocal consistency method effectively utilizes the 3D surfel map to enforce trifocal constraints across random pairs of images and map points, thereby enhancing the model's geometric understanding despite varying viewpoints.

In the context of multiuser MIMO, the task of jointly selecting users and precoding can be reformulated as recovering a group-sparse signal from underdetermined equations. Building on this reformulation, the paper introduces an efficient algorithm that exploits group sparsity in the relevant basis to achieve this recovery. The algorithm, iterative group matching pursuit, converges to a group-sparse solution at the edge of the feasible region for user selection and is a subset of feasible solutions. Its performance, however, can be enhanced through initial projection into the feasible region. The algorithm's performance was evaluated via both analysis and simulation, proving its efficacy in extending structured Compressed Sensing methods to the MIMO problem and potentially increasing the number of recoverable users.

We demonstrate that the rational function semifield of a tropical curve has a finite set of generators over a specific semifield. This involves identifying a particular finite set that generates the semifield. Furthermore, for finite harmonic mappings between tropical curves, the rational function semifield can be decomposed into a specific set of elements over a particular semifield.

This text offers a brief overview of mathematical techniques for identifying the steady-state distribution and dynamic behavior of a conditional process when a certain event doesn't occur, given an initial random state. We study the case where the event has a non-zero probability. We provide detailed analyses for both finite-state and infinite-state Markov processes.

We demonstrate that under certain conditions, the simple closed curve simplex's alternating sum consistently equals zero for a a particular type of Vassiliev invariant. Specifically, for unitary knots, simple closed curve simplex does not yield zero; however, we establish that for these knots, the vanishing condition holds for symmetric iterated derivatives that are permutation-invariant. Furthermore, we prove that for unitary knots with a given order, all less-complex unitary knots exist, enabling an equivalence between the order of invariants and the classical degree in unitary knots.

The connection between unconventional superconductivity, antiferromagnetism and nematicity, which are prevalent in iron-based superconductors and collectively referred to as Mott physics,, remains an unresolved puzzle in condensed matter physics.  The iron-based superconductor LiFeAs becomes superconducting below 8 K, and it is one of the very few antiferromagnetic and Fe-based superconductors, existing on the "liquid" side.  By introducing lithium into polycrystalline LiFeAs under high pressure of 5.5 GPa, we created a heavily doped, metallic and strongly correlated superconductor Li1+xFe4As4, which exhibits a superconducting transition at 42 K.  The metallic, "liquid" side of doped iron-based superconductors was thus extended to polycrystalline materials through chemical pressure.  The highly metallic, doped superconductor Li1+xFe4As4, which exhibits robust superconductivity at high temperatures, demonstrates anomalous nematic behavior under both normal and superconducting conditions.  The nematicity is further amplified by the proximity to a QCP in closely related, more heavily doped compounds.  The metallic, "liquid" side of doped Li1+xFe4As4, which is characterized by strong correlations and nematicity, represents a pivotal challenge in the study of high-temperature superconductivity.

This research reviews a global analysis of Type-II two Higgs doublet models and considers the impact of current and future experimental constraints on the model's eight-parameter space. The model's predictions for electric dipole moments and Z-couplings between light Higgs bosons are assessed in the context of the upcoming experiments. Furthermore, implications of these measurements are evaluated, and the constraints they impose on the two h Type-II model's parameter space are analyzed, with a thorough discussion related to Higgs boson production through vector boson fusion, future experiments expected to refine the Higgs boson mass measurements.

We demonstrate through simulated molecular surface experiments that neuroevolutionary learning can independently design particles and temporal processes for self-assembly into complex, "unseen" structures with high efficiency. By utilizing neural architectures and a mutation mechanism, our approach can uncover intricate self-assembling particle designs that surpass traditional methods in complexity and diversity. Notably, our algorithm can rapidly create novel particles capable of forming highly ordered, stable metastable states and temporal processes that form complex, chiral structures. Furthermore, our simulations reveal that collective behaviors of multiple design instances can be successfully modeled and replicated through simulated neural activity.

Our analysis centers on chiral gauge theories employing fundamental and anti-anti-fundamental (or symmetric/tensor representations), with the ultimate goal of developing a low-energy effective Lagrangian to understand lattice simulations of these theories displaying dynamical-Higgs-phase behavior as discussed in our previous work [arXiv:1705.06059]. The weyl anomaly effective action, when modified by a low-energy effective operator derived using the most general gauge-invariant method, accurately describes the dynamical-Higgs-phase lattice simulations, effectively eliminating the need for gauge-dependent terms in the gauge sector. An extended analysis of this approach even allows us to understand why similar efforts previously made by B. Holdom, as referenced in his Ph.D. thesis, failed to replicate successful outcomes.

This study investigates the properties of stationary solutions to the Navier-Stokes equations in multi-dimensional spaces with possibly unbounded domains. Under suitable assumptions that include conditions on solutions and their corresponding weak forces, we define a weak solution to the stationary Navier-Stokes equations in $d$-dimensional space for $1 \leq q < \frac{d}{2}$. For dimensions other than 3, we explore and analyze the existence of appropriate function spaces and the overall well-posedness of these equations.

We are studying the influence of non-linear interactions between magnons on the dynamic response of a specific class of magnetic insulators. The examination is conducted within the context of a specific insulator structure and involves the use of a theoretical framework based on spin waves and linear response theory. The analysis reveals a significant effect where interactions between different magnon modes lead to a non-zero polarization. The predicted polarization response can be further amplified through an external magnetic field and may be observable through specific techniques, such as time and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy and terahertz spectroscopy.

This research introduces two modifications for enhancing the security of Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem.
Originally built using Gabidulin codes within the McEliece framework, Loidreau's system is now susceptible to a polynomial-time key recovery attack under certain circumstances. To counter this vulnerability, we suggest the incorporation of a linear function, specifically a line, into the mapping, thereby prompting a generalized version of the Minimally Decoded Key Recovery (MDKR) attack. To further complicate matters, we also propose the integration of a random linear code into the keying process. To our knowledge, this is the inaugural application of the MDKR attack on code-based cryptosystems that employ unknown check matrices. The modifications we propose ultimately yield a modified variant of Loidreau's system that demands a significantly larger degree of minimum distance for secure communication, $t > 2, \sqrt{q+1}/2$.

To improve pre-trained language models (PLMs), we propose a new regularizer that 
helps PLMs learn robust representations by reducing their sensitivity to adversarial 
attacks through a novel adversarial regularizer. The method can be seamlessly 
integrated into existing models without necessitating changes to their original loss 
functions or data preparation processes. The effectiveness of our approach has been the 
subject of a comprehensive experimental evaluation that demonstrates its superiority in 
comparing state-of-the-art PLMs across various tasks. The empirical evidence indicates a 
notable improvement of 3.5% in robustness while maintaining accuracy of 1% or above in 
clean settings. The source code of our model can be found at: 
https://github.com/ashwini1111/RobustPLM

The minimum weight spanning tree in graphs and its generalization to the minimum spanning acycle on manifolds are explored. We analyze a scenario where the minimum weight spanning tree is computed using limited information about weights. Given a point process representing weights on a manifold, some of which are known, while others are determined through relationships with known weights and a transport map, we find that the empirical distribution of weights converges as the sample size increases. Additionally, the empirical sum of weights converges in distribution to a specific functional involving a deterministic function and a random variable generated from a Brownian motion on a Cayley tree.

In this context, Federated Learning is employed to process sensitive data while maintaining client confidentiality. This study explores the concept of applying secret sharing in the federated learning paradigm, initially addressing horizontal and subsequently vertical federated learning scenarios. Here, horizontal and vertical refer to the manner in which client data types are utilized. Specifically, horizontal federated learning occurs when clients have varying row numbers but share the same feature count, whereas vertical federated learning occurs when clients have the same number of rows but distinct column counts. Utilizing the approach introduced in previous research, we apply linear regression characteristics to maintain client data confidentiality. Here, the model is partitioned according to its coefficients using secret sharing techniques. This method ensures the secure aggregation step in Federated Learning, preventing server-side knowledge acquisition. Our study demonstrates the feasibility of this technique even when clients possess different data volumes. This study further examines scenarios involving multiple vertical clients interacting with a horizontal server, addressing the server's inability to infer client knowledge despite knowing column counts and feature counts for each column. Our study introduces a novel verification step essential for preserving client confidentiality in vertical federated learning. Our study formally proves the security efficacy of this method, addressing both confidentiality and integrity concerns.

A new, unique, weak interaction process is examined, involving the decay of $B$-Mesogenesis, involving $B$ mesons, baryons, and various baryon types such as protons, neutrons, nucleons, omegas, sigmas, upsilons, and phi mesons. Using the standard model, this reaction can occur due to Pauli exclusion principle and W-boson exchange. To produce the baryon asymmetry of the universe, a theoretical framework based on a dark Dirac fermion, $\chi$, is proposed. This model considers a freeze-in mechanism involving the interaction of dark fermions with the standard model Z-boson before and during the electroweak epoch, as well as within the standard model lpton sector. Additionally, this study investigates how these processes can potentially alleviate constraints imposed by dark matter observations and may be potentially detectable through future experiments involving baryon or dark matter detection.

In a Smart City, multiple interconnected systems operate simultaneously, posing a vulnerability to terrorist threats that aim to inflict harm while minimizing the chances of capture. To address this challenge, we have developed a bio-mimetic agent-based model that simulates the behavior of terrorists, citizens, and law enforcement officers during a attack. Our model predicts the likelihood of casualties and locations of incidents by analyzing interactions between agents. In response, we have also proposed a reactive decision support system that uses real-time data analysis and machine learning algorithms to guide strategic responses. In a study involving a simulated attack in a city layout, the results showed that a proactive approach significantly reduced injuries and fatalities compared to a reactive response.

Researchers examined the properties of spherically symmetric, charged black holes in an expanded space. By considering specific phase transitions similar to everyday substances, scientists discovered that black hole phase transition temperatures are directly related to pressure. Moreover, a diagram representing the mechanical stability of charged black holes matched corresponding states analogous to isotherms seen in ordinary substances. Furthermore, a calculation revealed that charged black holes remain stable in a part of their potential space similar to real-world isotherms.

Long document retrieval has been a longstanding challenge in both readers and comprehension models. State-of-the-art models often struggle with long documents as they are designed to focus on specific portions of the text in order to pinpoint answer spans. In contrast, recent research has found that incorporating temporal information, or understanding when events occur, can be beneficial. Our proposal addresses this gap by introducing a temporal retrieval mechanism, leveraging event time-mentions mentioned in the document. Event time-mentions provide crucial information to guide the model's attention towards the most relevant information to encode. We have incorporated this insight into our proposed method, called Temporal Relevance Model (TeRM), to enhance large document retrieval. We have successfully tested TeRM on multiple datasets spanning both print news and online magazines datasets across long and short document formats, showcasing its ability to outperform baseline models on various tasks.

The pseudo-labeling method has gained widespread application in unsupervised graph learning. Yet, pseudo-labeling strategies designed for Graph Neural Network (GNN) in node classification tasks often rely on the inaccurate labels generated by semi-supervised GNNs. As a result, they can't effectively address the issue of scarce, reliable labels. To rectify this limitation, we've developed a pioneering pseudo-labeling framework to address the problem of scarce, reliable labels in unsupervised GNN node classification tasks. The framework selectively updates a node's pseudo-label only when there's sufficient, reliable information available. To address the issue that semi-supervised GNNs tend to over-smooth node representations, making it challenging for them to capture informative node patterns and generate reliable pseudo-labels, we've developed a framework that combines the robustness of semi-supervised GNNs and the over pattern search capabilities of deep learning models. The framework iteratively updates a node's pseudo-label by a robust GNN, preserves the fine-grained patterns of node representation by a self-supervised model, and carefully assigns pseudo-labels based on a node's reliability and label dependency. The proposed method has been rigorously evaluated on various graph datasets, resulting in significant improvements over a wide array of alternative pseudo-labeling strategies.

Betatron radiation spectroscopy in a plasma wakefield experiment can serve as a powerful tool for analyzing witness electron bunches and determining their transverse movement and oscillations within the plasma. The study presents a method for extracting key parameters from the witness electron bunch in such experiments. The research involves a proof-of-concept study using a witness electron bunch to simulate and analyze synthetic betatron radiation spectra. The simulation shows that key parameters, including electron bunch parameters and plasma characteristics, can be effectively extracted from the resulting spectra. The proposed method offers a non-invasive means of validating the parameters achieved in plasma experiments.

This study introduces the first fully verified methods for privately learning decision trees in a hierarchical network setup. To achieve this, we developed an abstract framework for privately merging data partitions and applied it to two key algorithms: private decision tree finding and private cluster analysis. These methods can simultaneously produce accurate decision trees and divide data in a private manner across multiple nodes, making it possible for large datasets to be processed efficiently. By using these algorithms, large datasets can be analyzed securely and directly on multiple devices, avoiding the need to transfer data to a central server and minimizing communication costs.

We focus on the variational inference task of minimizing a R\'enyi divergence regularized with a constraint in the context of exponential families, and introduce an improved method that utilizes a second-order optimization algorithm in the natural gradient direction. Leveraging the information-geometric connection between Bregman divergences and Kullback-Leibler divergences, our novel approach can be seen as a second-order method in the distance given by the Bregman divergence. This method is analogous to Adam, but with a theoretically grounded notion of variance. Furthermore, our approach enables us to derive a continuous-time differential equation in the natural gradient direction, which corresponds to minimizing a time-varying R\'enyi divergence with a fixed constraint in the variational family. This provides a continuous-time limit of the L2-truncated stochastic variational inference algorithm, and facilitates the development of a time-discrete version of our method, effectively merging variational inference and continuous-time optimization.

This generalises the discrete Bayesian network class to the chain event graph class, retaining the Bayesian network's benefits for interrogation, propagation, and learning, while also accommodating more models with directed acyclic graphs structure, particularly those representing cuts in directed graphs, which inherently belong to the chain event graph class. A new, more intuitive interpretation of cuts within directed graphs is provided to enhance understanding.

In a Hilbert space, we develop a forward-backward forward algorithm for solving a convex minimization issue, incorporating a linearly time-dependent monotone cocoercive time-dependent subgradient field. This study also introduces novel forward-backward algorithms, including forward-backward flow methods, to resolve Tikhonov regularization in convex minimization and non-smooth convex constraint smoothing problems. These algorithms are then applied to solve a texture synthesis problem.

This study investigates how complex flocking formations can emerge in response to external stimuli. We model the behavior of basic particles in a confined area near a wall, where the particles follow specific motion rules that account for environmental obstacles and the particles' desire to move forward. Our simulation shows that the particles' natural behavior gives way to periodic patterns when influenced by the wall, which can be represented mathematically as different types of repetitive movements. Through further analysis, we are able to identify certain characteristics of these patterns that seem to have universal qualities regardless of the specific rules governing the particles' movement. Our work also reveals that the wall can cause instability in the particles' movement patterns, which can be traced through a specific type of mathematical transition that has been observed to occur at different points along the wall.

Within the framework of a kinetic energy driven superconducting mechanism, the effect of impurities on the transport of quasiparticles in cuprate superconductors in the superconducting state has been investigated, employing the nodal approximation. Results indicate an inverted shape in the microwave conductivity spectrum as it pertains to the temperature variations, mirroring patterns observed in the pseudogap regime. Notably, the magnitude of microwave conductivity exhibits a non-monotonic trend with increasing impurity concentration. Through the numerical analysis conducted, the observed patterns can be attributed to the interplay between different quasiparticle types, namely Bogoliubov quasiparticles and hybridized states, which differ in their scattering patterns due to impurities to varying degrees. A comparison with the conventional BCS theory shows that the inverted pattern cannot be accounted for without modifying the quasiparticle density of states, a change that may result from additional interactions, such as electron-phonon interactions, or other mechanisms. Furthermore, the effectiveness of the nodonal approximation in the context of the scattering rate is demonstrated through the examination of its validity.

This passage discusses an anisotropic curvature flow, referred to as a crystalline curvature flow. A comprehensive review of this type of flow is provided, focusing primarily on the initial value problem's solvability and well-definedness.

Our survival relies heavily on plants, and they're remarkably adept at adapting to changing environments through a process of gradual modification. Plants respond to stimuli by adjusting their growth through various mechanisms such as bending, curving, or branching, and this process is driven by auxin hormone signals that influence cell elongation rates. To study this process, researchers use growth models based on partial differential equations, where the growth vector is a combination of an internal structural influence and various environmental stimuli like light or gravity. A key challenge is incorporating the feedback loop between growth and the environmental hormone signal, and recent studies, like the work by Scherfel et al. (2015), aim to use momentum-based growth models, where the environmental hormone signal influences the total momentum and the inner structural influence acts as a form of memory or stiffness. This work investigates the properties of the resulting growth model by analyzing the behavior of the total momentum and the existence, uniqueness, and stability of the resulting growth dynamics, as the structural influence acts as a form of memory or stiffness.

It has been established that the SLE loop measure arises from Liouville quantum gravity disks in a specific manner related to conformal welding. Specifically, the boundary of the Gromov-Hausdorff limit is determined by independent SLE loops with varying radii, which leads to a specific conformal welding property satisfied by LQD isometries. Furthermore, this conformal welding property has been found to hold universally for LQD's boundary, yielding new insights into two-dimensional boundary value problems solved by conformal loop ensembles and providing explicit formulas for determining the corresponding quantum gravity transition.

The Image Biomarker Standardisation Initiative is a global partnership that strives for consistency in extracting biomarkers from imaging data to enable efficient and accurate research in medical imaging. One of its primary concerns is ensuring that biomarkers can be effectively validated and replicated, prompting IBSI to develop a task force focused on the quantifiers used in imaging analysis. This group is committed to promoting transparent, systematic, and efficient quantifier evaluation. Following validation protocols for ultrasonic atheroproteins, specific guidelines are recommended for further quanticifiers and general quantification methods.

We have examined the effects of high-spin nucleon and delta resonances on kaon photoproduction. By integrating these resonances, such as the N*(2100) and D* (3872), into a isobar model, we observed their impact on process amplitudes. When these resonances are included, their significant coupling constants result in a clear, distinct structure that aligns with experimental data. Conversely, omitting these resonations leads to amplitudes that are unable to fit the experimental data, indicating a clear discrepancy. Moreover, we have calculated radiative decay widths for these resonances, with our results suggesting a potential connection between the large decay width of the N*(2050) and its observed double-peaked structure.

This research describes the process of preparing the MORPH-II dataset comprising 55,134 images. The methodology section delves into the individual steps of the pre-processing sequence along with their corresponding statistical analysis. The pre-processing stage aimed to standardize the images within the dataset through a series of enhancements and modifications to both luminance and chrominance channels. The pre-processing stage of the dataset yielded a diverse range of success rates varying from 19 to90 percent overall, ultimately leading to a reduced dataset of 49,063 images after excluding the failed cases. The post-processing evaluation demonstrated an average gender balance of52 percent for the54,  features being analyzed.

Building upon our previous research, we present a plan to examine the possibility of primordial black holes (PBHs) serving as dark matter through analysis of microlensing phenomena. Specifically, we will leverage data from the Magma and AGILE telescopes to investigate gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) in an attempt to determine if they can be attributed to PBH mergers. Furthermore, utilizing a high-resolution simulation model of the solar system, we aim to investigate the potential formation of Kuiper belt objects as PBHs fall into gravitational singularities.

University administrators and educational researchers are deeply invested in understanding how students make enrollment choices, which can significantly impact class sizes, student diversity, and teaching quality. Students typically select their courses based on various factors such as required credits, scheduling conflicts, preferred time slots, and required prerequisites. Previous studies tried to address this problem by developing predictive models, but they failed to account for a student's overall enrollment schedule, resulting in inflated student levels in popular courses. A new approach, called URSA, uses unsupervised learning and simulated scheduling to forecast student enrollments at the course level, based on prior enrollments and metadata such as scheduling, required majors, and expected enrollment in time slots. Experimental evaluations of URSA on two educational datasets revealed that it produces accurate simulations of the average number of students per course, accurate daily enrollments, and accurate hourly distributions.

This study compares two algorithms that regulate vehicle platoon formation to counteract the effects of time delays caused by information exchange. We first present global results that demonstrate stability across different vehicle scenarios using a two-dimensional linear stability analysis. Next, to account for the complexity of real-world driving with multiple vehicles interacting, a multi-scale simulation analysis is conducted. Two distinct information structures are analyzed: one where the distance between vehicles is considered, known as the nearest neighbor policy, and another where the average headway is calculated through data averaging over a specified time period. To validate the findings, actual traffic data is utilized, showing significant differences in variability and stability when applying these two control policies.

One of the widely used techniques for machine learning problems, particularly in large-scale settings, is stochastic gradient descent (SGD). A variant of SGD can be executed in parallel using multiple GPUs, with each one processing an independent subset of data and updating its model independently before syncing with the others. However, this synchronization process can cause delays, limiting the technique's efficiency.

A new variant of SGD, known as CA-SGD, has been developed to tackle this limitation. By allowing GPU processing to continue without synchronization, CA-SGD allows for improved scalability, using a method called 'lookahead'.

To optimize communication, a 'lagging' technique has been introduced to reduce the frequency of required synchronizations. As a result, CA-SGD exhibits 'communication-avoiding' properties, with improved scalability, and its efficacy is demonstrated through experiments on data sets of varying sizes.

The widespread dissemination of misinformation through the internet and social media has led to a global issue, affecting how people perceive the content they encounter online. To complicate matters, the introduction of AI-driven fake headlines has made it increasingly difficult to discern the difference between genuine and fabricated content. Research indicates that the average person struggles to identify GAN-generated content in a substantial percentage of cases, highlighting a challenge faced by ordinary people in identifying fake content in general. To address this issue, researchers have been exploring potential solutions, including filtering mechanisms and fact-checking services, to help people discern fake content and combat misinformation. Furthermore, studies have shown that humans tend to distrust computer-generated content due to its unusual language, language patterns, and unexpected content choices. In an effort to contribute to the ongoing research in this field, our study focuses on exploring whether specific stylistic characteristics of computer-generated text can aid in identifying its origin, ultimately assisting in the identification of fake content. To achieve this, we developed a novel feature representation method based on n-gram frequency, along with two additional feature sets that capture vocabulary similarity, sentence structure, and overall language style. By combining these feature sets and training our models using our proposed method, we were able to achieve classification accuracy rates exceeding 90% in our experiments, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach.

In polycrystalline, amorphous, and ion-damaged Kitaev materials, we demonstrate
that a spontaneous chiral spin liquid may emerge from an in-plane global
symmetry break. For samples with partial Hubbard $U$ coupling, it is possible
that this symmetry is broken at the level of the in-plane magnetic anisotropy,
resulting in the stabilization of a chiral spin liquid within a finite-temperature
regime. For ion-damaged samples, magnetic anisotropy is also influenced by
the irreducible representation of the crystal's point group, and may result
from either an in-plane anisotropy, leading to a polycrystalline spin ice state,
or an out-of-plane anisotropy, leading to a polycrystallin N\'{e}el state.
However, in both cases, magnetic disorder caused by random irreducible
representations and the random anisotropic exchange interactions can result
in the stabilization of a chiral spin liquid within a temperature gap.
In both scenarios, low-energy excitations are characterized by Majorana fermions
coupled with a lattice of honeycomb fluxes, with interactions mediated by
out-of-plane magnetic fluctuations. This leads to a finite polarization aligned
perpendicular to the honeycomb plane and associated with a characteristic
magnon gap mode located at the $K$ point in the magnetic susceptibility structure
factor. This

Radio interferometry data processing can benefit significantly from the use of the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), a method often applied to two-dimensional arrays, extending its scalability beyond the limitations of traditional correlator architecture.  By using the FFT to calculate cross-correlations between array data, the total computations required can be minimized, achieving a scale of O(N^2 log N).  However, radio interferometry applications typically involve one-dimensional spectra, prompting an investigation into the potential for creating synthetic spectral data from interferometry data.  Our approach generates spectral estimates by applying smoothing across array data channels without the need for traditional imaging techniques.  We have designed an efficient algorithm to apply smoothing across array data, achieving a computational cost of O(N^2), and enabling simultaneous visibility calculation using the FFT at a cost of O(N^2 log N).  As a result, this hybrid system allows for the generation of high-quality spectral images at a lower computational cost compared to traditional methods.  We have demonstrated the potential of this approach through applications to various astronomical sources.

For several decades, the Markowitz mean-variance framework has been the standard for modern portfolio management. However, the increased volatility in markets and unexpected events like financial crises have rendered conventional generative models less effective. Unlike other generative models, we leverage the unique characteristics of financial time series by exploiting their inherent autoregressive properties using advanced generative adversarial networks. We introduce a Conditional Generalized Normalization Process (CGAN-P) for creating realistic stock market scenarios, incorporating Persistent, Skip-Gram Inference, Descriptive, and Adversarial network (CGAN-P/PGIN) components. CGAN-P outperforms the conventional Conditional Generative Adversarial Network (CGAN) in terms of accuracy, as assessed by the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test and RMSD analysis. Furthermore, our proposed Confidence Interval Generator (CGI) creates realistic time series within observed minimum and maximum bounds, leveraging a multi-head autoencoder to identify latent patterns and reconstruct original data. The effectiveness of the CGAN-P and CGI is demonstrated through the analysis of four distinct stock markets: US, Germany, Japan, and Australia.

We have derived the polarized massive operator matrix element $A_{gq}^{(3)}(N)$
analytically to three-loop order in QCD for arbitrary values of $N$,
including both single- and double-mass scenarios in the Larin scheme.
Additionally, the result is verified by its agreement with previous calculations
at lower orders and matches the analytic discontinuities obtained through a
specific method involving the imaginary part of the result at order two.
The result is also evaluated numerically and presented in a table,
including values of both the one- and three-mass cases $A_{gq}^{(3),1m}(N)$
and $A_{gq}^{(3),2m}(N)$ up to two-mass configurations.

A groundbreaking method to categorize Fermi-LAT blazar candidates has emerged, distinguishing between HBL and GBL types. Prior attempts to classify blazars have centered on data from optical and radio wavelengths, yet this study successfully utilizes gamma-ray data for accurate classification. The researchers developed a state-of-the-art deep neural network model using comprehensive data from the Fermi-LAT Sample Catalog, integrating morphological properties, light curves, gamma-ray spectral properties, machine learning-derived parameters, and shotgun spectra. The study demonstrated that shotgraph spectra yield better GBL/HBL classification results than morphological parameters, yet morphological data offers valuable insights into understanding blazar properties. Based on this study, the Fermi-LAT blazar candidates were successfully classified using the trained DNN model, revealing a preponderance of HBL candidates, which contrasts sharply with previous studies utilizing other wavelengths.

Active participation and user engagement are crucial components of social networking platforms, and various features are being introduced to facilitate self-expression and interaction. Beyond textual content, users now share images, videos, multimedia links, embedded media, maps, music, polls, and other rich media formats to express themselves. These innovations cater to users' varying preferences in content consumption and are expected to elevate social networking to new heights. This study examines the emerging trends in advanced social networking through the application of rich media features by thoroughly reviewing recent literature and providing a comprehensive analysis of the discussed media types. The review, conducted using a systematic approach, covers literature published between 2015 and 2020 and includes a total of 87 studies that explore rich media applications in social networking. The findings are based on key characteristics of the reviewed studies, offering insights into rich media feature applications and their impact on social networking evolution.

In this paper, we propose a new approach to defining hypergraph operations using tensors and demonstrate the equivalence of three formulations within this framework. We establish that any hypergraph can be viewed as a composition of hypergraphs formed by a common tensor-based operation. This operation allows us to identify and create novel hypergraph classes, enabling us to calculate various properties and identify existing operations within these classes without needing to refer to two-dimensional figures. We also explore the properties of hypergraphs formed by various tensor operations and demonstrate the ability to determine tensor decomposition.
