The CRESST experiment is capable of thoroughly exploring dark matter particles. 
To efficiently analyze all constituent parts of its apparatus, a multi-faceted 
approach is taken, incorporating thermal and radiogenic investigations. 
This involves performing nuclear measurements at accelerator facilities, 
assessing device performance under various conditions, and processing mineral samples. 
This study documents those accelerator tests and presents findings from CRESST-248.

Blind image deblurring aims to counteract the effects of unknown motion patterns that have been blurred into an image. This objective is often framed as a system identification challenge, where a combination of unknown impulse responses must be identified to accurately reconstruct the original image. In this study, we develop an efficient algorithm utilizing a new approach that utilizes a flexible kernel mixture representation of these responses. This new representation is achieved through the use of efficient factorizations and a stable method of determining the underlying basis set of these responses. Our new approach outperforms conventional methods in all scenarios and achieves significant computational speed.

This paper introduces a new concept called associative BiHom-Yang-Baxter pair with weight (λ,γ) which can be used to construct double curved Rota-Baxter system with the same weight (λ,γ) on an associative bihomogeneous algebra A. Furthermore, we establish equivalent conditions for the BiHom-Yang-Baxter pair and present its correspondence with curved Rota-Baxter structure. Ultimately, we demonstrate the modular data of the BiHom-type quantum group constructed from BiHom-Yang-Baxter pair.

Formal verification methods like static analysis offer developers reliable feedback, assisting in bug prevention, but correctly defining relevant properties relies on expert knowledge, making the process challenging to initiate. The creation of assertions in natural language that require automatic translation proves even more complex due to their vague nature, hindering effective static analysis. Our novel language Air addresses these difficulties, enabling users to write high-level specifications directly linked to code lines, with Hoare logic properties automatically generated and mapped to the source code. We validate Air's effectiveness through multiple cases, showcasing the benefits of formal verification methods when specifications are specified using Air, potentially shoring up code bugs and enhancing reliability.

Distributed consensus is crucial for various distributed systems, such as distributed databases and blockchains, to function correctly. The Canopus protocol efficiently handles the challenges of asynchronous communication and the random failure of network nodes. The protocol is based on a novel concept of weakly fair naming, reducing the overhead of communication. We present a simplified proof of Canopus' liveness, addressing a gap in the original publication where this liveness was unsubstantiated. The new proof not only fills this gap but also improves the overall efficiency of the protocol, significantly lowering its communication complexity without compromising its performance.

Recent studies have explored the introduction of cholesterol into pure phosphatidylcholine (PC) lipid bilayers through thermal fluctuations. By analyzing the spectral density and correlation functions using inelastic neutron scattering and small-angle neutron spin echo spectroscopy, respectively, researchers gained insights into the intermolecular interactions governing lipid bilayer dynamics. A cholesterol-free PC bilayer was compared with a 50 mol% cholesterol-containing PC bilayer to determine the impact of cholesterol on dynamic properties. It was discovered that the presence of cholesterol reduces the lipid bilayer's bending modulus but has no significant effect on its thickness or internal compressibility. Furthermore, it was found that the decoupling of lipid bilayer undulations and internal movements occurs when the molten-disordered state is reached, as evidenced by the loss of a power-law slope in scattering spectra and increased scattering signal at high frequencies. This phenomenon was also observed through enhanced spectroscopic signal, likely due to increased scattering due to small-scale density fluctuations within the bilayer.

This paper examines the loop quantum cosmological model generated from the ADM Hamiltonian. The model's cosmological dynamics are characterised by a critical matter density that prevents the big-bang singularity, regardless of the quantum parameters. Additionally, the density at which quantum gravity effects take over is also determined. The model is further validated by (i) matching the non-relativistic limit to the standard ADM formalism and the standard big-bang model, (ii) preserving the big-bang limit, (ii) preserving the bounce at zeroing of the Hamiltonian constraint, (iii) matching the expansion rate with the ADM formalism and quantum bounce models at the non-relativistic limit and (iv) matching the behaviour of the position and momentum of a particle at the non-relativistic limit. The model is found to converge to the standard cosmological model at its non-relativistic limit and to exhibit its full quantum corrections in loop quantum cosmology.

The Pierre Auger Observatory catalog details 100 extensive air-showers 
recorded between 2004 and 2020 for high-energy particles, spanning a specific
energy range from 78 to 166 EeV. This comprehensive dataset is made available 
for close examination, alongside nine events used to establish the energy scale 
for each detected primary particle. An accompanying plot displays the locations of 
these events on the sky relative to the detector.

Deep neural networks have become a prevalent approach in robotic systems due to their exceptional ability to process and analyze complex data. Nonetheless, their use in robotic systems is constrained by the uncertainty in their output predictions, as the standard used for assessing this uncertainty, called conformal prediction, is prone to inaccurate results when the distribution of the training data differs significantly from the testing data. This paper proposes an innovative method for generating uncertainty estimates from the output of deep neural networks. The proposed approach leverages latent representation learning and unsupervised density estimation techniques to create a robust uncertainty estimate that can withstand substantial discrepancies between the training and testing data. The method was assessed through the use of a self-driving car dataset and was demonstrated in a real-world robotic application. The outcomes of the experiments revealed that the proposed approach outperformed other state-of-the-art methods for uncertainty estimates.

The integration of advanced traffic monitoring systems has led to significant advancements in traffic data collection. Building on this, the development of traffic forecasting systems has gained considerable attention. The existing traffic prediction models have shown remarkable accuracy in providing accurate travel time predictions, which is crucial for traffic management. To improve traffic prediction robustness, this study proposes the use of spatially-cropped data in spatial temporal attention models. By breaking down traffic data into smaller spatial units, the proposed framework enhances robustness predictions across diverse datasets, offering significant improvements in travel time accuracy and providing a more accurate estimate of uncertainty.

In recent years, increasing research has been dedicated to studying higher category theory.
We've elevated Gray categories to the level of tricategories through the introduction of a strict morphism composition law, which we refer to as strict Gray categories.
We've also established an equivalent strict Gray category to any general Gray category, revealing that the process involves enriching the associativity and identity constraints.
We've further demonstrated that strict Gray categories hold a specific type of universal property, which establishes a relationship between Gray categories and premonoidal categories, which we've utilized to create a new strict morphism composition law in tricategories.
We've also found that strict tricategories form a full and faithful sub-2-category within the 2-category of Gray categories, which we've utilized to establish the equivalence of Gray categories and tricategories.

Hippocampus segmentation is crucial in diagnosing various neuropsychiatric conditions,
such as Alzheimer's disease. Recent advances in deep learning have led to improved
performance in segmentation tasks, particularly through the adoption of U-Net's architecture,
although its performance is compromised by data augmentation. A new approach has been
developed to enhance hippocampus segmentation accuracy using a hierarchical learning
method for deep networks. By combining low-resolution training with high-resolution
inference, hierarchical learning allows models to leverage the benefits of multiple scales,
improving their ability to process high-resolution input data effectively. We have validated
the efficacy of this method in hippocampus segmentation, using U-Net and Mask R-CNN models
and evaluating their performance on the Structural Equation Learning Alzheimer's Dataset.
We further explored the impact of hierarchical learning on multi-task learning involving
segmentation and volumetric measurements. We observed that models trained without data
augmentation but with hierarchical learning performed comparably to those trained with
augmentation at multiple scales, offering potential benefits in models' adaptability and
transferability.

We've developed an experiment that brings together the principles of quantum theory and Einstein's theory of relativity. Our research builds on the concept of quantum contextuality by merging it with the fundamental principles of the relativity of timeframes. We found that when setting up a complex interference scenario involving two path options involving three parties, none of whom share the same path, is achievable using the principles of classical relativity but is impossible without applying quantum relativity principles. Our experimental findings demonstrate clear evidence contradicting the relativity of quantum systems' 'being in two places at once' property.

Our research provides a detailed analysis of the composition of protons in Earth's inner radiation belt, focusing on data collected between 2012 and 2016 by the NASA RBST instrument, which measured flux levels at varying resolution. The examination separated the inner and outer radiation belts using specific energy thresholds, revealing a significant difference in spectral characteristics across this boundary. Notably, findings suggest that electron scattering is likely responsible for contributing to the formation of the inner radiation belt's intense proton levels. Additionally, analysis of the outer radiation belt showed that while initial formation may occur through adiabatic processes at certain altitudes, this phenomenon transitions into a different formation mechanism above approximately $3.4R_E$, where pressure-cycloidal resonance with $m = 1$ at $M_{min} \approx 17.5$ MPeV is proposed as a potential cause.

A network's expressivity is a crucial factor in determining deep neural networks' potential for excellent generalization performance. Recent research has sought to expand the concept of expressivity beyond the simplistic terms of high or low, and investigate its nuanced variations. This paper investigates how expressivity affects the optimization landscape and the final network configuration obtained through training. Furthermore, experimental findings suggest that certain slow-learning patterns are critical for achieving the best possible generalization, which in turn relies on the expressivity of individual network layers.

This research investigates a more secure variant of low-rank matrix completion that
protects data using differential privacy. A central challenge involves private
estimation of key matrix matrices given $M$ observations of $XY$, where $X\in
{\mathbb R}^{n\times m}$ and $Y\in {\mathbb R}^{m\times p}$ are independently
subject to the Gaussian mechanism of privacy. Our proposed algorithm uses the
Huber estimator, achieving a dimension-dependent error rate $\tilde O((np/m)^{1/2}
R^{1/2} n^{-1/2})$ for the Frobenius norm, matching existing results but
utilizing fewer samples, especially when $R \ll n/(np)^{1/2}$.

We propose a novel approach for creating detailed isotopic maps of interstellar dust by applying a dynamic model of gas-phase ion-molecule reactions to interpret observations. In our model, heavier ions are assumed to be linked to dust particles, while their lighter counterparts are freely floating in the interstellar medium. The model incorporates a series of complex reactions that occur between these ions and surrounding gas molecules, allowing us to identify gas-phase precursors of specific interstellar dust species, including polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, silicates, and water ice. By integrating this dynamic model into an existing radiative transfer code, we are able to generate isotopic feature maps that align with existing data and help us better understand the composition of interstellar dust particles, which in turn influences the evolution of cosmic chemical elements.

Research on exoplanets orbiting low-mass stars is particularly significant, given their extended duration of core contraction. To better understand the formation and evolution of planets in these systems, we conducted a hydrodynamic simulation and conducted an analysis of the evolution of a planet around a 0.095 M☉ star.
Using the results of our simulation, we analyzed the system's development and the potential formation and evolution of a planet in a circular, 15.5-day orbit.
Our analysis revealed that a planet with a mass between 1.5-50 M⊕ would form and reach equilibrium in an eccentric orbit, achieving a circularized orbit within 1.5-1000 million years, depending on its mass.
However, very massive planets and large solid bodies that form in this system are unlikely to survive due to gas disk evolution and planet-planet scattering, respectively.
Consequently, our study supports the idea that super-Earths and mini-Neptunes are found in nearly circular orbits around low-mass stars, particularly those within 100 days, indicating a significant discrepancy between observed systems and predicted initial eccentricities.
Furthermore, our study suggests that a system where 100 low-mass stars and their planets are observed would reveal a system where 10 M-star system and their associated planets in nearly circular orbits would reveal a system where a planet with a minimum mass of 1.5 M

Consider the following modification to a game of lights called Zero Game. It's played on a graph, where each vertex has an on/off state for a light. When a player selects a vertex, the light turn on for that vertex and its neighbors, if they weren't already off. A player makes an optimal move if they can follow a sequence of moves to turn off all the lights that were initially on. This modified version is known to not always have an optimal move available. We define the closure of a graph, denoted by $\mathcal{C}(G)$, as the maximum number of steps required to solve any configuration of lights on $G$. We show that $\mathcal{C}(G)$ is at most the chromatic index of $G$. Additionally, we provide examples to show that $\mathcal{C}(G)$ is at least the size of the shortest path on $G$ plus 1, and that some graphs exist where $\mathcal{C}(G)$ is strictly in between the chromatic index and the size of the shortest path on $G$ plus 1.

This paper presents a novel, multi-task deep learning model that integrates image segmentation and image restoration tasks. The approach relies on connected components theory to ensure the preserved shapes within segmentations remain closed sets under continuous transformations. We introduce two new regularization methods that employ shape preservation, which not only enhance segmentation accuracy but also enable the concurrent training of image segmentation and image restoration tasks. Our novel framework enables the effective resolution of interdependent challenges at the interface of image segmentation and image restoration, a combination that we call imgsegion, where imgsegiation represents the removal of high-frequency noise and dependency, leading to more coherent and accurate shape-based segmentation results. The proposed model's performance in ultra-weak light conditions and digital camera removal of JPEG artifacts demonstrates its effectiveness.

Program analysis through Abstract Interpretation involves simulating the behavior of a program in a simplified environment to approximate its true behavior. This simulation traditionally has two steps: the upward phase uses approximation to ensure the analysis stops, followed by the downward phase which uses interpolation to mitigate the loss of accuracy caused by earlier approximations. This paper suggests an alternative by temporarily ignoring properties that lead to infinite loops in the analysis, thereby dynamically adjusting the approximation level. The proposed technique is formally applied to the computation of fixed points, providing a method for dynamically interpreting functional languages with mu-calculus semantics.

In recent years, topological phonons have received significant attention due to their emergence within certain material structures such as YMo4SyO10, GaCu2-TeO2(Ga), phononic crystals, and strain-engineered films. We investigate a broader phenomenon by incorporating MO4SyO10 (where M is Si, Ca, Sr, Zr, Ca, Zr, Mo, and Sy is Cl, Br) into their frameworks and demonstrate through computational analysis that all these 24 materials possess topologically non-trivial arrangements due to their formation of a phononic gap near the $\Gamma$ point in their phonon band structures.

Unsupervised outlier detection in various fields such as data mining and machine learning relies heavily on distance-based methods due to their adaptability in outlying anomalies identification without requiring specific data distributions or feature independence. Despite the development of numerous algorithms using distinct strategies, the field still lacks a comprehensive evaluation framework. The primary objective of this study is to propose a thorough evaluation protocol for benchmarking unsupervised outlier detection algorithms based on diverse distance metrics. The proposed framework involves selecting and evaluating 23 state-of-the-art algorithms using a collection of synthetic and real datasets for different criteria, including data dimensionality and class distribution variability. The assessment encompasses a comprehensive analysis of algorithm performance, resource efficiency, and scalability. The initial results highlight the importance of validating algorithms using both synthetic and real datasets, as well as the potential for improved benchmarking through the use of collection-based and ensemble-based approaches. The recommended protocols and associated tools are available online at the provided URL.

The probability of (g)aussian random walk paths for an g(e)xcited atom approaching the vacuum side of a conducting plane has been evaluated to determine its impact on the atomic spontaneous emission rate when the atom is near the plane. Key factors influencing this rate include the distance between the atom and the plane, as well as the frequency or wavelength of the photon emitted during excitation. A comprehensive analysis of the derived probabilities reveals significant insights into the behavior of spontaneous atomic emission under these conditions, potentially offering valuable practical applications in related scientific inquiries.

As applications relying on graph representation learning grow, we examine the performance of GNNs in generating fair predictions. The particular scenario of neighborhood fairness, where predictions by nodes with the same features are aligned with their connected non-friends, is investigated. With the nodes in a network serving as agents and the edges representing social ties, our focus lies on the fundamental fairness challenge that emerges from neighbor relationships. The distributed nature of this problem presents distinct challenges, which we overcome by proposing an algorithm that is resistant to unfair nodes initiated from the user's neighboring relationships. The effectiveness of our solution is demonstrated on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

This research focuses on applying modern analytical techniques to kinetic models of reversible enzyme reactions. Despite the effectiveness of numerical methods in obtaining exact solutions to these models, they often struggle to provide insights into the behavior of systems with multiple time scales. To address this, we apply the simple structure preservation (SSP) and homotopy perturbation (HPT) methods to derive approximate solutions of the rate equations governing both single-substrate and multi-substrate reactions. These methods yield algebraic equations representing the system's long-term behavior. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we compare it with other analytical and numerical methods using numerical simulations.

A well-studied model for the decay of the gluino through intermediate squark states has received less attention than other scenarios. This scenario is characterized by the final state consisting of six light neutral particles and low missing mass, making it difficult to detect at the LHC using current methods. However, with enhanced detection sensitivity and multi-jet plus missing energy analysis, we find that this scenario, though extensive in gluino mass - potentially exceeding 2.5 TeV, results in identifiable gluino pairs with a minimum invariant mass of around 400 GeV, which translates to a gluino mass greater than 800 GeV. Furthermore, with upgraded detector capabilities to capture lower mass jets and missing energy above 200 GeV, we predict that we can discover this scenario even if the gluino mass exceeds the gluino's energy by a significant margin, effectively rendering it unbounded.

This research examines the characteristics of financial market behavior when multiple types of arbitrageurs engage in trading activities with differing risk tolerance levels and views on future outcomes. Focusing on the conditions that allow for financial bubbles to form and persist, the study reveals that these conditions are influenced by heterogeneity in the traders' risk tolerance levels as well as their cross-sectional risk preferences. To explore these interactions, the paper examines a two-period, riskless asset model where multiple arbitrageur types with differing views on future returns and varying degrees of caution in trading exist. Findings suggest that financial bubbles can emerge in relatively competitive markets even if the price of the asset deviates minimally from its fair value, while the presence of significant risk-aversion in the traders' interactions exacerbates the conditions that allow for bubbles to form. Moreover, the results highlight that even the presence of multiple arbitrageur types increases the conditions that allow for bubbles to emerge in the market.

Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either steady-state driving forces varying in intensity or driving forces that changed over time. Calculations of position expectations in the ground state showed linear relationships with the forces for both types of cases. Similarly, positions of the wave functions' minima correlated with the driving forces and followed parabolic patterns. Constant analysis of the potential and kinetic energies revealed that these energies increased and decreased respectively. When examining the kinetic energy, it was found to have higher values at lower and then higher potential values, creating a symmetric distribution. In addition to the aforementioned findings, it was also discovered that the kinetic energy peak shifted towards lower potential values when the potential was changed.

This study proposes a novel approach to predicting ratings in a recommender system by integrating the concept of item sentiment using natural language processing techniques. The method capitalizes on the relationship between user mood while watching a movie and its rating potential. The system's rating prediction capacity relies on the presence of sentiment-driven movies watched by the user. The approach employs a UV matrix for prediction, where U and V matrices are populated by identifying users with high sentiment scores associated with a particular item. The research involved creating a sentiment lexicon by parsing IMDb item descriptions through stemming and identifying positive and negative words. The implementation utilized a Python-based sentiment analyzer to evaluate the sentiment of movies in a sample dataset. The success of each user in predicting a movie's rating was determined by their average sentiment score. The outcome indicated that when a user viewed multiple high-sentiment movies, they had the ability to predict those movies' ratings accurately. The approach was validated by comparing its prediction accuracy to that of collaborative filtering methods. The implementation was performed on a dataset containing 2300 users who had rated 1707 TV shows and movies.

One key obstacle in natural language processing for multilingual texts is the lack of data, a significant issue particularly prevalent for code-switching texts. This is particularly evident in texts that seamlessly blend languages, like those found in South Asian countries, where the text often conveys the same meaning in either language individually. Our study aims to develop a subword-level bilingual model for code-switching by employing a subword-level word alignment model and training it with mixed data. This novel method allows the training corpus size to be several times larger than is currently feasible.

We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly irreducible, cannot be endowable with a certain type of near-invariant metric.

We're investigating integrable boundary conditions within certain types of conformal brane geometries, such as AdS x R^4 and AdS x H^4, as well as their product forms AdS_p x H_q. Our focus lies in the study of a specific class of geodesics that maintain their integrability under these scenarios, utilizing the properties of geodesic motion in curved spaces. An important outcome of this research lies in the discovery of new points of integrability, extending our comprehension of conformal brane geometries. Furthermore, our findings allow for the creation of novel solutions to the sigma-model with curved space targets, leveraging the constraints imposed by integrable boundaries.

In numerical simulations, hexahedral mesh elements are commonly used. 
We develop an algorithm to create hexahedral meshes for arbitrary quadrilateral 
shapes and implement it in C. 
The algorithm is divided into two parts - fixing mesh singularities and 
subdividing the mesh. 
The algorithm begins by translating the mesh vertices to eliminate edges within 
the triangle formed by the vertices. 
Next, we develop a method to subdivide the mesh by connecting opposite edges and 
repeating the process until the mesh is fully subdivided. 
The algorithm handles complex topologies and is suitable for use in parallel 
computing.

The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a
common challenge, as defined respectively by identifying relationships between
entities or predicting unconnected entities within a graph. A novel approach, known as
LAPLACE-KG, employs a unified model to address both tasks by converting extraction
into a relationship prediction problem. The model leverages a graph-based
embedding for entities and incorporates modified graph connections to encode
potential relationships, allowing it to dynamically adjust its focus towards unresolved
relationships. Through experiments on four datasets, it has demonstrated
LAPLACE-KG's capability to significantly outperform existing models on both related
tasks with notable improvements in accuracy.

This study introduces an innovative analytical delay model specifically tailored for deep submicron CMOS inverters. Developed based on the critical recognition that inverter delay is a complex interplay of multiple process variables and load capacitance, the proposed model incorporates parameterized equations derived using Curve Fitting Toolbox in MATLAB. By training the model with varied technology nodes and inverter stages, and subsequently verifying it with different well isolation processes and diffusion regions thicknesses, the analytical delay model was shown to accurately predict delay with respect to width, length, and load capacitance. Notably, the model's ability to accommodate diverse nodes and structural configurations makes it versatile and easily extendable to other deep submicron technology nodes and similar system designs.

This module's learning methods assume the smoothness of Q-functions, using the estimated metric, and can adapt to cases with or without smoothness assumptions, as they can handle both scenarios. It supports the four common performance metrics, including discrete and continuous Q-values, and different measures of expected total or discounted return. The brain's ability to distinguish between living and non-living objects within the ventral temporal cortex has given rise to two potential explanations: a gradient theory suggesting a continuous difference and a distinction theory indicating separate categories for living and non-living objects. We investigated these theories' validity by analyzing neural activity data from individuals undergoing brain surgery and discovered that both theories can seemingly account for this neural differentiation of living versus non-living objects. However, it's crucial to recognize that both explanations rely on identical underlying evidence, which might be due to confounding factors, necessitating the need for novel experiments to clarify this phenomenon.

In scientific simulations, various approximation techniques, such as finite element and finite difference methods, are employed to estimate key characteristics like concentration or temperature distributions. These traditional methods often rely on higher-order continuity and may have limited applicability. This paper introduces a new class of approximate filters that do not have such restrictions, enabling the estimation of nonlocal functionals directly from numerical solution approximations. A novel stabilized finite element method is used to compute the approximate estimates, providing improved accuracy in the presence of discontinuous coefficients in reaction-diffusion problems. The proposed method's effectiveness is demonstrated through theoretical analysis, numerical optimization examples, and comparison with standard approaches like the finite element method with Graded-Diffusion.

Quasi-periodic oscillations type-C (QPOs type-C) have been observed in several black hole X-ray transients and are believed to occur in both the hard and soft states. We conducted the first detailed analysis of QPO type-C utilizing data obtained with the eX-ray Timing and Spectroscopy Mission, which provided high-quality timing and spectral data of the black hole Cygnus X-1. Our results reveal the presence of QPO type-C within a 0.03 to 0.05 Hz band during the transition from the hard to the soft state in the source and suggest that the oscillations are driven by changes in the innermost region of the accretion disk.

In the context of multi-agent reinforcement learning, particularly for cooperative settings, researchers have explored a novel approach to measuring how much MiMARL algorithms rely on team coordination. This involves developing two metrics to quantify how much a policy is optimized for coordination versus individual rewards. These metrics aim to pinpoint any inherent preference for team rewards and detect possible vulnerabilities to coordinate with malice. Experiments have shown that several MARL algorithms, including MADQL, MAPPO, and MADDPG, exhibit a preference for individual rewards, leading to suboptimal performance when forced to coordinate. This issue of relying on coordination strategies can also be exploited by malicious agents within the environment.

We introduce MatSim, a comprehensive benchmark and dataset for visually recognizing materials, offering a wide range of, to-date unseen, training examples for the material class. Visual material recognition, a seemingly simple task, is crucial in, for instance, home automation and virtual fashion. Visual material recognition, however, is a particularly challenging object recognition task due to the vast number of materials and their subtle, intricate differences. Advances in neural networks have enabled machines to tackle this task effectively, yet current models are limited by the small number of examples per training material, leading to overfitting. Furthermore, current datasets are restricted to a narrow range of materials, often distinct from the materials they are designed to classify. To combat overfitting and enhance generalization, we develop MatSim, a novel approach and extensive new dataset consisting of 16,000, three-dimensional materials and comprising 200 distinct material classes. To maximize the potential of MatSim, we devise a novel, advanced machine learning model based on self-supervised learning, achieving a 2x improvement in performance compared to current approaches. To facilitate efficient use of MatSim, we provide an easy-to-use API and web interface, enabling users to search, manipulate, and modify the dataset materials. Our new dataset is now publicly available for research at the MatSim website (matSim.ai).

Two equivalent formulations of Lie 2-algebras are recalled: one as a categorification of Lie algebras and another as 2-term L∞-algebras. The paper proceeds by introducing four different types of Lie 2-algebras derived from 2-plectic manifolds, Courant algebroids, homotopy Poisson manifolds and multivector fields on Poisson manifolds.

We introduce a novel method for local image feature matching, particularly in low-texture areas where traditional descriptor-based approaches often fail. Our method leverages a Transformer architecture to identify and connect semantically significant features across images. We utilize widely available open datasets to train the model end-to-end, enabling it to adapt to various image pairs without requiring a tailored approach for each dataset. Our proposed solution surpasses current state-of-the-art models in matching features from highly textured images, such as those found in the ImageNet database.

The widespread issue of bias in high-resolution magnetic field maps obtained from high-resolution spectroscopy, particularly affecting the component of the magnetic field perpendicular to the line-of-sight (B⊥), persists. This issue was first identified in earlier studies and has been linked to the way stellar spectra are modelled. To further investigate this problem, high-resolution magnetic field maps were reconstructed from observed images. The results from polarimetric data analysis showed that the existing bias in B⊥can be significantly underestimated due to the presence of magnetic field regions inclined at an angle to the line-of-los. To accurately represent these regions, high-resolution magnetic field maps need to be deconvolved of the existing bias. Several methods were developed and evaluated to achieve this goal.

This research paper explores a real-world scenario in which consumers fail to negotiate with the electricity provider, resulting in an inability to reach mutual agreement. To address this challenge, we develop an analytical framework that effectively models the electricity provider's and consumers' interactions through tiered pricing strategies that incentivize consumers to shift their peak-energy consumption during off-peak hours. The scheme's effectiveness is further enhanced by incorporating an adaptive mechanism that adjusts pricing levels based on the consumers' responses. To simulate and assess the electricity provider's and consumers' behaviors, we construct a mathematical model that accounts for the consumers' responses to the scheme and varies their demands in real-time. An optimal optimization model is formulated to determine the pricing parameters, employing novel mathematical tools to simplify the problem and efficiently identify the optimal solutions. The model's performance is validated via case studies, demonstrating its capability to achieve two key objectives: 1) achieving mutual agreement and agreement satisfaction between the electricity provider and consumers; 2) maximizing the electricity provider's revenue.

The generalized form of the Einstein theory, the Rastall theory of gravity, incorporates the conservation of the energy-momentum divergence. By introducing a black string into this framework, its radial component is considered to define the thermodynamic properties, including Hawking temperature, entropy, free energy, and other thermodynamic potentials. Calculations are initially performed in four dimensions, then generalized to $D$ dimensions. The findings reveal that the behavior in five dimensional spacetime differs, suggesting the significance of this distinction when analyzing black string thermodynamics.

The results demonstrate that the power-law decay rates found in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem for discrete systems directly correspond to pointwise scaling rates of a spectral measure with a spectral value of one. Moreover, assuming weak convergence, when no spectral gap is present, the convergence rates of the time-average in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem rely on sequences of infinite time as they tend to infinity.

The research on metal-poor halo stars offers crucial insights into the Galaxy's chemical evolution and star formation history. A particularly notable star is found in the OGLE-TR-188 exoplanet system, which has an unusually high abundance of strontium, barium and oxygen. This study investigates further and finds that OGLE-TR-188 is an unusually rare r-process star within the thin disk population. Its unique chemical composition suggests it formed from a single small supernova event in the thin disk, which occurred less than 1 billion years after the thin disk initially formed. This rare event was not reflected in the overall abundance of the thin disk, implying the supernova's yield was only a small part of the total mass of the thin disk.

This research examines the temporal evolution of global and regional fire seasons using a novel methodology based on daily global fire locations and associated areas burned, as presented in the NASA FIRMS database. We identified the spatial distribution and temporal patterns of fire seasons across seven distinct regions: the Americas, Europe, Asia, Africa, and polar areas. We found that in most regions, the majority of annual fires occur during a concentrated period. We calculated the probability of encountering large fires, defined as those exceeding the regional median fire size, and observed significant variations in these probabilities both spatially and temporally, especially in areas experiencing fires in the southern hemisphere. We generated a high-resolution (25 km^2 resolution) historical record, spanning from 2003 to 2020, characterizing global fire seasons, their probability distributions, and associated extremes. We further investigated the characteristics of fires in the late 2010s, analyzing their occurrence rates, spatial patterns, temporal distributions, and duration. We found that in the late 2010s, the majority of fires in the southern hemisphere were unusually short, with median and mean fire durations significantly lower than in the previous decade. Moreover, we observed fires occurring earlier in the year than in the past, with in-year distributions deviating from historical patterns. We attribute these observations to potential climate influences, including increased rainfall and prolonged wet periods, in the late 2010s.

We've conducted a thorough examination of seven previously proposed metrics for measuring the morphological complexity of it/noun phrases. These metrics either directly quantify the morphological properties of phrases or measure the inherent variability within the morphology of a single phrase. Our research employed a multivariate statistical analysis across approximately 100 thousand Italian noun phrases to assess the reliability of these metrics. The results show that all metrics are internally consistent and significantly correlate with each other, although they may be influenced by external factors such as word length, the length of stems, the type of morphological category, the length of morphological category, word entropy, the entropy of morphs, and the entropy of whole phrase. A principal component analysis reveals that the first component, which accounts for approximately 80% of variability among the metrics, combines the reliability and diversity aspects of the vocabulary of single word.

A crucial examination of dark matter subhaloes is presented in the context of understanding self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) as a possible solution to the "small-scale crises" of standard cold dark matter (CDM) models. Using the same set of 1000 CMC subhaloes identified in the simulation of CDM-2 from the previous study, this research extends the findings to the SIDM models, including models with and without velocity dependence and to a range of interaction strengths. Employing a modified approach to model SIS cored subhaloes, this research provides a comparison of the CMC and SIDM models' characteristics such as mass profile (M_200 and M_500), concentration, and mass. The results show that SIDM substructures tend to have less steep density profiles, resulting in cores of lower mass than their CMC counterparts, and this effect increases as the dark matter particles interact more strongly. Using a modified profile to model SIDM models, this research found that the core-saturation mass is weakly dependent on these interactions. However, when considering the same set of CMC and SIDM models' characteristics, this research found that SIDM models tend to have more massive cores and less steep density profiles than their CMC counterparts. This effect increases as the dark matter interactions become more frequent and stronger.
