In contrast, Orion A's UV continuum showed dust contributions significantly redden the continuum, comparable to or exceeding those observed in the Milky Way's average levels. Furthermore, UV continuum observations revealed a distinct break at an wavelength of approximately 160 Angstroms, likely due to absorption by the Lyman limit. These findings provide valuable insights into the UV opacity of the Lyman limit and the scattering properties of the interstellar medium.

Structured tables in various domains, especially in scientific research, efficiently present complex information in a compact format. However, they often go unnoticed in research on understanding unstructured text, limiting the full exploration of its insights. Our research identifies the key elements of table content, breaking it down into individual cell units, and categorizes each cell's role through analysis of its structure and context. By conducting extensive human evaluations, our extended data set reveals notable disparities in existing table understanding benchmarks, and we introduce a new evaluation track for table understanding in human-AI interactions. This novel task assesses AI's ability to fill missing table cells based on provided inputs, such as table structure, cells, and question-scaffolded queries. The extended dataset is publicly accessible at https://table-struct-recognition.github.io/.

This study introduces an innovative dynamic cognitive hierarchy theory that utilizes multi-stage games of incomplete information to model learning behaviors. Our model assumes players initially engage in learning phases where they gradually acquire information about the types of players they will encounter in the main game. As players' types become fully revealed by the end of the learning phase, the main game ensues. During the learning process, players construct and refine beliefs about their peers' types and actions. It is demonstrated that these beliefs converge, ensuring that established solutions for games of incomplete information can be applied to the main game. Notably, our theory provides new applications for solution concepts such as sequential equilibrium and Bayesian Nash equilibrium, enabling the analysis of dynamic cognitive hierarchies within a comprehensive learning framework. This approach also facilitates an examination of group dynamics and facilitates relative learning between groups.

Accurate and dependable population data is vital for governments to formulate and implement policies, particularly in areas such as vaccination programs and the design of infrastructure. Although census data offers a regular and reliable estimate, it is often unattainable for many regions due to the unavailability of comprehensive data collection efforts. To address this issue, satellite imagery has emerged as a potential solution for monitoring and counting populations continuously and without interruption. Our research focuses on leveraging machine learning techniques and remote sensing data to consistently and reliably estimate population estimates using modular and scalable data collection methods. To showcase the feasibility of our approach, we have conducted case studies on several cities around the world, demonstrating state-of-the-art results in population estimation.

Over the past ten years, significant research has been conducted to design efficient methods for testing approximate membership within limited timeframes. The existing approaches have primarily centered on standard hash tables and a variation called cuckoo filtering. This paper reveals the underlying mathematical principles governing such structures, enabling the creation of novel filtering techniques incorporating advanced hashing methods like Treap. Furthermore, we introduce the application of a non-uniform random function in cuckoo filtering, yielding improved results for reduced false positive rates. Our experiments demonstrate a significant decrease in storage and processing times for optimized structures.

Our theoretical analysis examines how Bose-Einstein condensates and their hot counterparts interact through spin collisions and light absorption. We found that the way these particles lose energy heavily relies on how long it takes for they become associated with each other via these collisions. We also discovered that the time needed for this process impacts the speed at which hot particles disappear. Moreover, the time needed for this to happen has a direct influence on how rapidly atom-molecule pairs are produced when starting with zero-energy atoms and how this pairs' number grows over time.

The field of fluid-structure interaction involves complex simulations that can be efficiently addressed using multi-resolution techniques in the Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) framework. This framework is particularly well-suited for fluid-structure interactions due to its ability to naturally handle free-surface boundaries and moving interfaces. In this research, different multi-resolution techniques are applied to 2D and 3D simulations of linear waves and ship wave patterns to evaluate their effectiveness and efficiency. A novel approach combining 2D SPH with a grid-based adaptive technique and standard h-, p-, and r-refinement is developed and implemented. This is complemented by the development of special boundary treatments and a robust mesh-particle coupling method ensuring efficient and accurate data exchange between particle-based and grid-based meshes. The research demonstrates that multi-resolution algorithms can achieve significant speed-ups (up to 10-20 times) over traditional high-resolution simulations while maintaining high levels of accuracy.

Due to the quantum nature of quantum systems, they can naturally represent complex patterns with high information density, potentially giving us the opportunity to leverage quantum computing's inherent efficiency in representing high-dimensional machine learning models.  This work introduces the concept of quantum gradient descent, where a gradient descent process is implicitly performed on a quantum device, potentially allowing for more efficient computations, especially in scenarios involving data representation.  We explore the conditions under which quantum gradient descent offers efficiency, introduce various quantum algorithms that can be part of this process, and compare these algorithms to their classical counterparts.  We also analyze the benefits and constraints associated with employing quantum gradient descent and present our perspective on the current state of quantum machine learning.

A recently created TTS model called FastPitch can change pitch, but the resulting speech sounds unnatural when modified pitch is used. To overcome this limitation, our work develops an alternative method by combining FastPitch with a modified algorithm that keeps vocal characteristics intact during pitch adjustments. Our system takes TTS output as input, shifts pitch, and then uses an acoustic voice toolbox to ensure consistency in tone and style. Our approach was tested with the TIMIT dataset, and our results show significant enhancements in the voice quality score compared to FastPitch, and even other leading methods in the field.

This research focuses on advancing object-based video reasoning research. The key challenges involve identifying the presence of objects, their existence over time, and the objects involved in specific actions. To address these challenges, we propose a novel end-to-dense relation prediction model called EPVRn, which targets the EPVRn Task: identifying relationships between object appearances and actions. The model employs a Object Re-identification module with an attention mechanism to ensure consistent object representation across multiple clips and is accompanied by a supporting Theorem confirming its effectiveness. Furthermore, we executed additional experiments and fine-tuned the our model on the well-known MSRCMT, UCF101, and Kinetics-400 action recognition benchmarks to validate the benefits of object re-identification.

Our study investigates lepton-pair production accompanied by bottom quarks at the Large Hadron Collider using theoretical predictions. By employing fixed-order perturbation theory and controlling various simulation parameters such as PDF tolerance, we assess the impact of different next-to-leading order corrections and evaluate multiple PDF4HCDD groupings. Additionally, we investigate the significance of bottom-quark effects in the Drell-Yan process and propose an optimized analysis strategy for the underlying event that incorporates a new, underlying event variable. In a simulation based on 150 inverse femtobarns of data at a 13 TeV LHC, we analyze how different PDF groupings and theoretical choices influence the sensitivity to the standard model and beyond-the-standard-model new physics, and how this impact varies with different lepton-pair mass regions.

Remote-controlled vehicles called Telepresence robots have gained widespread adoption in various settings due to their ability to be controlled over regular internet connections. Researchers are particularly interested in these robots as a means of evaluating the Quality of Experience (QoE) for remote navigation applications. By analyzing the feedback loop between the user and the robot, they found that the entire system can be considered a translation channel, with the quality of communication directly impacting the overall experience. Using this understanding, they developed a simple evaluation method for remote navigation applications, which involved applying the Blau-Diamond metric to measure the overall quality of the interaction. They then evaluated this metric on a group of Telepresence robots and found it effective in identifying issues with network connections. Furthermore, they proposed an extended version of this metric to better capture the nuances of the navigation experience.

In this study, we revisit the core features of the Bayesian adaptive Lasso method initially developed by Han and Hu (2012) for adjusting a hierarchical model under a large-n, small-p setting. This method involves defining a hierarchical model with linked hyperparameters, incorporating regression coefficients for distinct groups of factors, each with its own set of hyperparameters. We incorporate frequently used prior distributions for these hyperparameters. We incorporate a regression-wide Lasso into this framework. We discuss how to expand this method to accommodate various loss functions and covariance structures. We demonstrate that this method maintains the key properties of the Bayesian adaptive Lasso, including a consistent ability to identify the model and an effective error estimate. We also discuss a specific application focusing on hierarchical clustering with a shared regression-wide Lasso. This method relies on an EM algorithm to carry out the Bayesian inference. We use this method in simulations and a real-world dataset.

The game Mafia's underlying mathematical structure is still shrouded in mystery, 
despite its widespread popularity. To gain insight into this puzzle, researchers 
recently developed an algorithm that simulates the Mafia game and allows for the 
collection of data on its outcomes. The simulation allows us to investigate the 
relationship between mafia members' numbers and their likelihood of winning, 
revealing a crucial finding. Specifically, our analysis shows that as mafia 
numbers increase, both mafia and non-mafia groups' chances of winning follow a power 
distribution. The power parameter, notably, is around 1.8. Furthermore, our 
simulation reveals likely winning scenarios, specifically, 4 mafia members and 1 
or 2 non-members. The findings also suggest strategies for mafia members to gain 
winning advantages, such as leveraging their first night's discussion and the 
second day of discussion opportunities.

Researchers aim to understand how and when giant planets develop a core and obtain gas, as well as the impact of gas availability on their mass ratios. A statistical analysis of planets from 119 systems with a planet detected by the Radial Velocity method revealed information about the mass ratios of adjacent planets. It was discovered that the distribution of mass ratios is not solely determined by orbital separation but rather by the timing of gas accretion, which occurs earlier for inner planets. In models where planets form within their gas disk and migrate, planet masses decrease with time, whereas in models of in-situ formation, gas accretion occurs from the inside out, aligning with the findings. However, further investigation is required to fully grasp planet formation processes, including gas accretion dynamics, migration, and stopping mechanisms.

The electrical conductivity of a solid is heavily influenced by phonons and is a key indicator of its electrical transport characteristics. While previous studies have shown the presence of phonons using infrared spectroscopy, they have not been able to quantitatively analyze the phonon contribution to conductivity. This letter presents a demonstration of using inelastic phonon scattering to measure the phonon contribution to electrical conductivity in a nanomaterial, specifically graphene nanoribbons, via ultrafast phonon pumping. Our results provide an estimated phonon contribution to conductivity of around 100 S/m and reveal a multi-peaked conductivity profile with distinct features for each material's bandgap phonon mode.

This research introduces a novel fuzzy k-means approach tailored for high-dimensional data, referred to as the Weighted Fuzzy k-Means with Dynamic Feature selection (WFFBSDF) algorithm. Distinguishing itself from conventional Fuzzy k-Means methods, WFFSDF offers the ability to: 1) identify the optimal clustering configuration by calculating varying importance levels for individual features; 2) assign features different importance based on their individual contributions. We formally define the algorithm's algorithmic structure and provide an analysis of its time and space complexity. Empirical evaluation of WFFSDF is conducted across multiple datasets with diverse feature counts and object quantities to assess its clustering efficacy and effectiveness in feature dimensionality reduction. We further compare the proposed algorithm with standard k-Means and fuzzy k-means methods in terms of clustering distance and selected feature dimensions.

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have been widely used across diverse fields, but existing learning algorithms suffer from high theoretical computation complexity, limiting their practical application. This study proposes an efficient algorithm to quickly learn MoE parameters, demonstrating significant speed improvements on standard benchmarks, while maintaining or even enhancing model performance. The developed algorithm leverages task embeddings to minimize overhead on standard cross-entropy loss, enabling rapid and effective MoE parameter learning. In contrast to traditional methods, which require extensive background calculations, this algorithm achieves comparable model accuracy with reduced model performance loss, often less than 5%.

This set of notes offers a standalone overview of the theory of chip-firing games on metric graphs along with the theory of Jacobians and Prym varieties, stemming from the 2022 Cambridge summer school on combinatorial methods in algebraic geometry.

While both particle physics and cosmology utilize global symmetries, their applications diverge significantly due to differences in typical energy scales and observational methods.  As global symmetries offer the potential for more precise theoretical modeling, the pursuit of their effective mathematical representation is of particular interest to mathematicians.  To address this, researchers have developed novel methods for identifying and parameterizing symmetries within differential systems, which can be applied to the effective field theories of particle physics and cosmology.  This text presents an overview of these methods, highlighting their mathematical foundations and practical implementations.

Our research presents the findings of our spectroscopic examination of ten blue horizontal branch stars within the Milky Way's globular clusters from the LAMOST-SGaia-RRD survey. By analyzing these objects, we identified three potential reverters, a newly recognized type of blue horizontal branch star, supported by our derived parameters and spectral analysis. Our research also includes a study of three blue straggler stars, which were found to have masses approximately 0.2-0.3 times that of a solar mass greater than those of their horizontal branch counterparts. As a result, we categorize these objects as blue stragglers rather than late reverters. Furthermore, we provide a list of basic physical properties, such as temperature, surface gravity, and metallicity, which align with previously published data for these clusters. Our data on these objects is made available in the form of extended HRD entries and will contribute to the understanding of globular cluster populations and dynamics.

This note presents a new category of broken submersions with coloration and orientation, which extends the b-principle and encompasses directed piecewise smooth submersion maps, initially defined by R. Bland in 2010.

The goal of deep transfer learning is to leverage pre-trained deep neural networks (DNNs) on natural image datasets for downstream tasks. These pre-trained DNNs are often transferred to downstream tasks using task-specific fine-tuning. Despite their effectiveness, these pre-trained DNNs lose some level of generalizability to downstream tasks for which they weren't trained. To address this limitation, our work reveals the latent potential of cascade neural inductive representations (CNIRs) as a method to enhance the generalizability of these pre-trained DNNs. This involves using inductive representations (IRs) to guide DNNs through a process of gradual, multi-stage domain adaptation. By applying this CNIR framework to pre-trained DNNs for downstream tasks, our research demonstrates that this method significantly boosts generalizability by nearly 10%, making it a more robust solution for open-set scenarios. This new framework, Cascade Neural Inductive Representation (CNIR) learning, serves as a strong baseline for enhancing the generalizability of these pre-trained DNNs.

In various scenarios, such as marketing campaigns, technological advancements, and spreading ideas, understanding how information spreads is essential. Our study explores how the structure of networks, specifically their modular composition, impacts the speed and breadth of information spread. By applying time-dependent community detection algorithms to noisy data, we found that modularity hinders information flow, resulting in slower diffusion and more concentrated initial growth. This phenomenon, dubbed the 'modularity bottleneck,' is most pronounced when the noise level is low, causing the initial spreading hub to be trapped in the largest module before the information eventually reaches all nodes in the network.
Under specific conditions from Floer theory, we introduce measures to gauge how close two Lagrangians lie to being orthogonal within their respective surfaces.

The reliability of a discrete-time channel model that uses a standard method of perturbation
is numerically investigated for cases without signal amplification. We assess the size of
discrete nonlinear interference to find the longest time period over which signals remain connected.
The strength of this interference to time of interference ratio is crucial in assessing the
accuracy of this model. Two methods of determining the estimated period - fitting a pattern and
analyzing the differences in successive data points - are examined along with their prediction
errors. Two different types of nonlinear models show the same model period determination
sensitivity to the presence of noise. In both cases, increasing the gap between data points
reduces detection errors, but ultimately limits the estimated time period's size. Two distinct types
of detection errors are studied: accurately predicting the detected period length and identifying
the actual period length present in actual data.

The widespread adoption of Android devices has led to an increase in malicious software due to their ease of replication and rapid malware development outpacing security measures. Although network-based evasion attack countermeasures have been developed, research on problem-space attacks targeting Android malware detection remains limited. Problem-space attacks exploit the limitations in APK analysis techniques to conceal malware behavior. To combat this, we propose a new type of countermeasurable attack called sample reconstruction, which can reconstruct theApk's layout without altering its functionality. By demonstrating data reconstruction in both single-sample and dual-sample activation evasions, our research reveals a key vulnerability in current Android malware detection strategies.

Service-oriented computing has been utilizing the service concept for nearly two decades, and over the course of this time, significant progress has been made in automating service interactions through web services. However, the fundamental notion of a service as a black box has remained unchanged despite these advancements. This paper suggests that with modern service technologies, it's now feasible and advantageous to move towards a "transparent box" model in which the internal workings of service-oriented systems can be directly accessed and inspected.

Recent Hall conductivity measurements at a heated TeO2 crystal surface revealed an exotic particle-hole symmetric topological order. The research suggests that this phenomenon arises from a unique state where quasiparticles have an effective negative charge. To study the topological properties of this state, researchers have proposed a model Hamiltonian consisting of an artificial spin glass. The Hamiltonian's structure reflects that of a Heisenberg model with modified interactions and an added term representing the quasiparticles' negative charge. The model's phase diagram shows that, in contrast to classical spin glasses, certain regions are dominated by external magnetic fields, leading to distinct phases. These distinct phases have significant implications for thermal Hall conductivity and topological order at the testQS surface, potentially explaining the measured phenomenon.

Our analysis indicates that Thakurta black holes cannot exist due to unrealistic requirements related to charge density, and thus, we reject their consideration as dark matter candidates, aligning with previous research by S. Henshall.

The formation of planets, particularly the rapid growth of solid particles within certain regions of dust-rich protoplanetary discs, is a highly active area of research. A particular mechanism called gas trap formed by long-term gaps and pressure ridges in these discs, may facilitate rapid core formation. To investigate this further, researchers are using various simulations to study how dust particles accumulate in these pressure ridges. A recent study incorporated two types of simulations to examine the effect of varying dust growth rates and gravitational influences on disc gaps. The results showed that dust can accumulate in certain parts of the disc, even without significant radial migration of dust, particularly when the width of the gap is less than certain disk features like a ring of accumulated dust. However, dust migration towards wider pressure bumps in the disc, caused by differences in grain growth rates, can limit core formation and instead potentially result in ring of accumulated dust that splits the disc into multiple rings and rings of dust.

In almost all machine learning, parameter-efficient approaches have been thoroughly investigated. This paper, however, explores computational constraints in the context of two-bit weights. It demonstrates that computational limitations make it impossible for any learning algorithm to replicate the outcomes of more complex models, regardless of their complexity. Similarly, parametric approaches are shown to be ineffective at solving the same problem under the same constraints. These findings shed light on the challenges underlying parameter-efficient learning and suggest future research directions.

Given countable discrete abelian groups, compact Hausdorff groups and their dual groups, as well as already fixed probability measures on their dual groups, we find specific conditions that enable us to prove that, for certain subsets of the group, there exists a non-trivial Bohr set within the sum of the subset with its statistical inverse. These conditions enable us to solve a conjecture proposed by Sarnak, in which we show that, under certain symmetries, the properties of the group's elements relate to its correlation with moebius, which ultimately leads to an improved version of the von Neumann-Weil conjecture. Consequently, our findings allow us to identify generalizations of pretorsion groups within semilinear groups of type $GL_n(q)$, in addition to rectifying an error found in an earlier paper of Davenport and Haran.

This study addresses the dial-a-ride problem within large urban settings where residents have multiple transportation options at their disposal. To remain competitive, ridepooling services must balance high pool participation rates with minimizing detours for users. However, current solutions often rely on inefficient branch-and-bound algorithms that rely on time-discretization, which significantly hamples their ability to process large numbers of requests. To overcome this limitation, this paper proposes a novel two-stage heuristic approach that utilizes advanced route optimization techniques. The first stage generates high-quality solutions for smaller problem instances, which can then be used to train a machine learning model. The trained model can subsequently provide near-optimal solutions for much larger problems in a matter of seconds, utilizing only the initial solutions as starting points. The effectiveness of this approach in delivering initial solutions of high quality is demonstrated through comprehensive testing.

This study explores multi-modal pretraining techniques in the domain of E-commerce. We identify key challenges associated with the modality, encompassing issues such as cross-encoding accuracy due to diverse data types, the substantial imbalance between classes, and significant missing datasets. To address these difficulties, a novel dataset involving 200 million samples, known as E-commerce Maxpretrain (EMX), has been developed. We propose two datasets, including Customer click history (CCH) and Product search ranking list (PSR), showcasing distinct characteristics. We propose two datasets, CCH and PSR, showcasing distinct characteristics. We introduce a data processing pipeline that facilitates data augmentation, involving operations such as embedding downsampling, negative sampling, and further downsampling at the embedding level. We devise various tasks including theoddy and contrastive learning. To tackle the challenge of negative examples, a specialized method called hyper-contrastive contrastive learning (HCL) has been developed. We conduct experiments using the proposed E-commerce Maxpretrain dataset and OMXL model. Our research demonstrates that our model achieves state-of-the-art results, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach and the superiority of our data and task design.

A significant function in a deep learning model is to generalize and adapt to diverse data and experimental setups. A new approach, Deep InfoMax (DIM), has been developed to address this challenge by introducing an extra dimension to the loss function, incorporating the temporal or spatial derivative of the model parameters. This results in enhanced data efficiency and a stronger link to brain imaging analysis concepts.

Text classification can be a difficult task, as models often struggle to accurately predict classes, relying on the presence of specific words. If these key terms are frequently absent from new data, the issue becomes even more pronounced. To alleviate this problem, we introduce the influence score, a novel word-level metric designed to identify texts based on distinguishing, class-relevant words that are also likely to appear in texts associated with the predicted class. A high-level interpretation of the metric reveals its ability to provide a concise summary of the texts linked to a predetermined class. Additionally, we show how the I-score can be utilized to enhance the reliability of word-level predictions made by imperfect text classification models. Experiments were conducted on various text classification tasks to validate the metric's effectiveness and also assess its potential to set "in text" thresholds that are relevant to text classification tasks.

We investigate the relationship between spin-orbit coupling and interactions within a two-orbital Hubbard model on a square lattice. We apply mean-field theory to determine the system's phase diagram, focusing on the competition between ferromagnetic and charge-order states influenced by the ratio of spin-orbit to interaction strength. We discover that the effective spin-orbit coupling within the magnetic phase is not simply proportional to the model's spin-orbit coupling constant. We find that the effective spin-orbit coupling can surpass its constant value when the interactions become stronger, potentially leading to a topological non-trivial phase dependent on the system's parameters.

A dark matter candidate that is long-lived has distinct implications for when it decays or ionizes the early universe, thereby affecting the structure and evolution of cosmological objects over time. Generally, if the dark matter candidate's mass is significantly lower than twice the electron mass, it is likely to have ionized the universe, and if it were present before the formation of the first stars and galaxies approximately 130 to 500 million years after the big bang, it could potentially be constrained by observations of these early celestial bodies. Furthermore, observations of these early stars and galaxies can also set stringent constraints on dark matter that is stable or long-lived and may not have ionized the universe, and this applies to a broader range of dark matter masses than what is typically constrained by other methods.

To ensure that AI-powered medical devices achieve accurate results in real-world settings where their training data may differ significantly, their performance needs to be evaluated when encountering such variations. This research proposes an approach for automatically identifying and testing medical devices' resilience to specific types of distribution differences. By utilizing a framework for inverse scaling, our proposed method enables real-time testing of a wide range of distribution differences by simply defining an inverse scaling transformation that reflects the expected shift in real-world settings. Such transformations can be derived from various sources, including changes in image composition, shifts in sensor values, changes in background features, and variations in object characteristics. By employing a template-matching technique, our approach can accurately predict the specific transformation applied to the training data and generate test images reflecting the desired distribution difference. As a result, this method offers a versatile and efficient way to rapidly test the distribution resilience of AI-powered medical devices.

The most reliable nucleic acid simulations that account for all atoms, mainly rely on empirical forcefields, limiting their dynamics to specific directions. While previous studies demonstrated the ability to regulate four or five rotational degrees of freedom through non-markovian force modifications, we introduce a novel method to fully control the complete set of rotations affecting the simulation. The approach utilizes time-dependent modifications to the underlying force, resulting in a nonlinear, time-dependent, non-linear differential equation. The solution to this equation is essential to determine the trajectories necessary for a successful modification. The method has been successfully applied to various DNA and RNA molecules, yielding the anticipated results. The study provides an open-access implementation of our approach, available at https://bitbucket.org/martinsan/ctrl_dna, and offers valuable insights into exploring complex nucleic acid structures, self-assembly, and system exploration. The method may also be applicable to other areas, including data-driven design and exploration of high-energy states.

The Asymmetric Numeral System (ANS) is a highly efficient, integer-only lossless compressor that achieves a low redundancy of $\sigma/\log_2 n$ bits per symbol. However, ANS encoders that use uniform initialization can incur additional redundancy. In this paper, we prove that using a precise ANS encoder's tail state distribution, the redundancy is only $c_1/\log_2\sigma + c_2\sigma/\log_2 n$, where $c_1, c_2 > 0$. This result confirms that precise ANS encoder tail state distributions asymptotically reduce the redundancy to $O(1)$ for any alphabet size. The derivation involves analyzing the ANS encoder's and decoder's tail state distributions as difference equations, and then solving for their steady states, which provides the basis for the redundancy proof.

Our approach integrates the effects of ion correlations into calculating liquid dielectric responses based on circuit theory. By developing a new dynamic model that includes these interactions, we have created an analytical algorithm that optimally fits experimental data using a simple network. This method successfully identifies the constitutive parameters of the corresponding circuit model and provides meaningful dielectric responses for a variety of liquids. Specifically, we have obtained encouraging outcomes for solutions containing monovalent cations and anions at different temperatures and concentrations, and our approach has offered new insights into dielectric breakdown concentrations of these solutions. On a theoretical level, our results demonstrate validity within low to moderate concentration levels by connecting with existing theoretical predictions derived from continuum-based methods.

In our research, we explore the possibility of forming heavy-diquark, heavy-triquark, and heavy-tetrabaryon molecules with spin-flavor structure, particularly focusing on their interactions. We utilize the non-relativistic quark model combined with a harmonic oscillator to study the properties of these systems. We also calculate the masses, root-mean-square radii, and decay widths of the tetrabaryon molecules and compare the results with those of certain known hadronic molecules, such as $X(3872)$ and $Z_c(3960)$, as well as other heavy-antiheavy molecules. The data presented in our research can potentially serve as a reference for the identification of heavy-nuclear-like molecules.

Research on military drones is growing in interest due to the rapid advancements
in control algorithms and the low cost of hardware, leading to the development
of software and hardware with impressive capabilities. The integration of
artificial intelligence in military drones is a cutting-edge area of research.
A significant number of papers using artificial intelligence in military drones
is being published, with a notable surge in 2019-2020. A distinct gap exists
in the field regarding the use of artificial neural networks (ANN) in
military drones. An investigation into the field revealed a notable interest
in 2019-2020, with a significant focus on military drones utilizing artificial
intelligence and high-tech hardware for data collection. A survey of scientific
papers using the most cited method, revealing a notable gap in the field
regarding the use of artificial neural networks (ANN) in military drones.

We employed Markov-Chain Monte Carlo analysis to investigate the impact of the Lyman-$\alpha$ three-dimensional correlation function on cosmological parameter constraints. We compared parameters derived from using Lyman-$\alpha$ and WMAP data alone, and in combination, with and without an additional constraint from the Lyman-break ultra-violet flux power spectrum. This comparison allowed us to assess the distinct information provided by different probes. We found that incorporating Lyman-$\alpha$ correlation function data significantly improved our constraints, roughly by a factor of 2. Our findings suggest that the Lyman-$\alpha$ three-dimensional correlation function is particularly sensitive to the cosmological parameters it traces, while the Lyman-break ultra-violet flux power spectrum provides complementary information. Our results indicate that future experiments, such as the High Resolution Imaging Spectrograph, will be able to break degeneracies between cosmological parameters and significantly improve our constraints when combined with other datasets.

Researchers at Fermilab have successfully conducted an experiment where a beam of particles undergoes an unconventional manipulation, swapping its horizontal and longitudinal beam patterns at the A0 Photoinjector. The new experimental setup, utilizing a specially designed deflector that resonates with the beam's frequency, forces the majority of the beam to decircle and collide with a target, leaving behind an enhanced beam with significantly reduced emittance.

Pedestrian tracking technology plays a crucial role in various fields such as surveillance, navigation, and security, prompting the growing need for more efficient and accurate prediction systems among commercial applications. Existing solutions, primarily reliant on computer vision techniques, have made notable advancements, but the need remains for continued improvement. To address this, we developed a novel computer architecture, Aras, designed specifically to accelerate a cutting-edge vision-based trajectory prediction model. This model leverages transformer-based architectures and multi-scale convolutional networks. By implementing Aras with its integrated components - including 1D convolution, positional encoding, self-attention, and spatial attention - on the platform a significant performance breakthrough was achieved relative to existing CPU and GPU implementations, namely speedups of 3.81 and 6.66 times respectively, and an overall speedup of 9.22 times when processing trajectories on Aras was achieved.

We present an enhanced version of Hebbian learning, capable of both increasing
and decreasing the complexity of a neural network, building upon existing research
that revealed Hebbian learning tends to increase neural network complexity over time.
In contrast to degenerate results from prior studies focusing on complex networks with
multiple time scales of connections, our proposed learning rule achieves stable
balancing of complexity under conditions of random and random plus random training data. Specifically, we demonstrate that by introducing a learning rate scaling factor inversely proportional to the total synapse weight magnitude, we can attain zero average complexity growth. Furthermore, this control mechanism ensures the stability of the learned weights and prevents the average complexity from fluctuating indefinitely. Our comprehensive scaling rule and its implementation on a neural network modeled after the XOR problem demonstrate its efficacy in complex pattern recognition.

This paper showcases initial research on an innovative technique for controlling a collective of robots via hand gestures captured by a depth camera. To validate this approach, a developed method is examined in conjunction with a previously established ROI detection method, a simpler technique that identifies key areas within the frame. A relevant computer vision algorithm is employed to analyze the captured hand data and classify it into recognizable gestures. We examine two classification methods: the former utilizes gesture libraries, while the other relies on a machine learning model trained to recognize gestures. Our results demonstrate that the approach based on the deep learning method yields superior performance compared to the alternative.

The study aims to assess the performance of composite deep learning models consisting of Recurrent Neural Networks and Convolutional Neural Networks for identifying diverse White Blood Cell types, a feat that could revolutionize automated medical diagnosis and blood analysis in pharmaceutical and healthcare settings by analyzing image samples, thereby aiding in disease diagnosis and drug development.

A key advantage of counterdiabatic protocols in driving quantum states is the ability to implement rapid changes while minimizing the impact of swift Hamiltonian modifications. The challenge lies in finding a Hamiltonian that accounts for all system degrees of freedom during a unitary transformation, which can be impossible for complex many-body systems or open closed-chain configurations. This paper demonstrates that a different strategy can be employed to achieve rapid, adiabatic-like state transitions in such systems. The approach involves using a simple, fixed quantum state as a reference to establish a mapping between initial and final many-body states, which enables the efficient insertion of a "quantum tunneling" term into the many-body Hamiltonian. This method is particularly useful for manipulating initial and final states that cannot be represented in fixed quantum states and may have broader applications in efficiently executing many-body unitary transformations.

Image processing applications such as satellite imaging, fingerprint identification, and medical diagnostics generate vast amounts of image data, necessitating efficient compression techniques. This research introduces a novel compression approach based on singular value decomposition, which incorporates 2D Discrete Cosine Transform and Gamma Mapping to improve performance. By replacing a traditionally used identity matrix with an optimised matrix in the SVD process, the proposed method outperforms existing compressive approaches in terms of Mean Squared Error and Peak Signal to Noise Ratio.

This research develops an expression to decompose infinitely differentiable complex-valued functions into a sum of exponentials along with a corresponding error term. Building upon this, a corresponding infinite series of exponentials is derived and found to be convergent under certain conditions, thereby yielding a corresponding approximating function with diminished error. A corresponding estimate is also established for the remainder term involving a specified number of terms. Additionally, bounds are set on the magnitude of complex variables based on the target approximation's accuracy standards. Finally, this work is adapted to the realm of stochastic calculus by expressing infinitely differentiable complex-valued functions of multiple variables as a sum of exponentials with an estimated error term.

Given a surface S equipped with a metric d, such that it meets the conditions set by Alexandrov for an upper curvature bound, we demonstrate the existence of an almost conformal harmonic map from d to the two-dimensional Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^2$. In cases where S exhibits almost nonnegative curvature, this map is shown to be conformal, except at a finite number of points. Notably, this result holds without imposing any constraints on the topology of S, and it is analogous to previous findings for Riemannian metrics, referencing key work by Lohvainen, M\"aki-M\"akinen-M\"aki.

The linear photon-photon fusion process (Breit-Wheeler process) involving a projectile and a target photon in the laboratory frame was studied with the incorporation of external fields. By applying a non-covariant approach, the differential cross sections for various photon energies and electron-positron pair production angles were calculated in the context of the laser intensity and its impact on polarization effects. An in-depth examination of the highest allowed nuclear charge was conducted along with the influence of external fields on various scattering outcomes.

A novel approach is introduced to map the parameter space of the Two Higgs Doublet Model (2HDM) based on its 13 key parameters, with a focus on 8 on-shell masses and 5 mixing angles comprising one primary ($\sin\beta$) and four secondary mixing angles. This map is primarily defined by comparing the strength of the coupling of neutral scalars to gluons and photons with the equivalent particles in the Standard Model, with the leading order ratio parameters denoted as $m_{12}^2 = \Lambda^2 \kappa_1 \cos\beta\sin\beta$ or $m_{12}^2 = \Lambda^2 \kappa_2 \cos^2\beta$. The ratios are constrained such that $\kappa_i = 0.1$ or $-0.1$, with $\Lambda = 10$ TeV, under the assumption that Type-II Yukawa couplings dominate in 2HDM. The study also considers scenarios where the pseudoscalar mass ranges from $100$ GeV to $10$ TeV, with the aim of identifying opportunities for future collider experiments to further constrain the parameter space.

We examine the RDF data exchange process based on relational data, employing the OWL 2 RDF Schema language for tuple-generating dependencies as constraints. Unlike previous related work utilizing OWL 2 DL, our approach can address more intricate RDF class and property restrictions, including those that are undecidable in general data exchange settings. A notable contribution is the development of typed RDF 1.1 IRIs, which are classified as data values instead of ensembles of such, allowing for the representation of IRIs within the RDF Data Dictionary through the use of bnodes. This distinction enables the formulation of decidable, parameter-free TGA dependencies, providing a significant advantage over similar work focused on OWL 2 DL. Additionally, we introduce a normal form that encompasses OWL 2 RDF Schema property restrictions, in contrast to related work that could only handle sources without such restrictions, which limits data exchange decidability.

A new field within econometrics is rapidly gaining momentum, centered around the topic of non-parametric and semiparametric production sets, supply curves, cost functions, price indices, efficiency, productivity, and stochastic frontier models. This burgeoning field is heavily influenced by non-parametric estimation and multivariate order preservation methods, and has significant implications for both theoretical economics and practical applications such as supply chain management and cost minimization. This scholarly monograph aims to introduce these emerging research areas, providing cutting-edge approaches and innovative solutions to longstanding issues in efficiency and productivity analysis. It covers a comprehensive range of topics, including non-parametric envelope estimation, entropy-based production functions, robust productivity and efficiency measurements, network production systems, choice problems, input substitutability, input complementarity, price indices, stochastic frontier models, and their applications. By integrating these diverse research areas, this comprehensive volume serves as an invaluable resource for researchers and practitioners.

We've developed a novel technique for reconstructing low-mass scalar boson production paired with a top quark and a W boson at the LHC for both proton-proton and proton-proton-run-2 conditions. Our technique yields improvements in mass reconstruction precision with the following reductions in mass resolution: 2.25 GeV for proton-proton-run-1 and 1.22 GeV for proton-proon-run-2.

Pre-trained language models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in capturing deep semantic relationships in local contexts, although their ability to represent hierarchical syntactic structures, inherent in pre-training objectives, is unclear. To investigate this knowledge, we examined how HuggingFace models' syntactic properties, utilizing standard syntactic parsing metrics and discovered the following: Linear projection matrices in relation to self-attention mechanisms are highly correlated with syntactic parsing performance. When combined, these matrices enable accurate syntactic parsing across various architectures, implying self-attention can internalize hierarchical structure. Conversely, other model components like embeddings and linear projections related to predictions do not exhibit the same effect but can be used to predict the syntactic tree's local properties. Our analysis also revealed self-attention can be employed to derive attention heads that serve as initializers for efficient attention-based parsers, resulting in improved parsing efficiency and accuracy across various models, sometimes surpassing existing pre-trained language model-based parsers.

The accuracy of speech recognition heavily relies on high-quality training data. A significant challenge in improving German speech recognition systems lies in the scarcity of available training data. Our study fills this gap by leveraging the publicly accessible data from the Spoken Wikipedia Corpus. This novel training data is compared with the existing high-quality COVIL data within the framework of the widely-used Websprach GmbH's Monotonic and CoVoST2 DNN-GMM hybrid systems. Our findings demonstrate that using Wikipedia-derived data surpasses COVIL in terms of performance. Moreover, we found that combining data sources yields even better results than employing data of the highest possible quality.

A comprehensive study examining 32 Be-type stars, a subset of the broader population of B-stars, utilized data from the VizieR catalogue, revealing that these stars are relatively uncommon, comprising only 0.7% of all B-stars. By analyzing rotational velocities, we discovered that Be-stars exhibit faster rotation rates than their B-star counterparts, with estimated averages of 240 km/s and 180 km/s respectively. Further analysis suggested an adiabatic rate of electron degeneration corresponding to a quarter of the nuclear rate, while calculations based on mass properties of Be-stars pointed to a central neutron star surrounded by a large, rapidly rotating envelope made up of ejected nuclear material.

To translate ASR output into written text, inverse text normalization is required, which our proposed solution achieves through self-supervised learning combined with deep transfer techniques. Our approach yields improved accuracy over previous state-of-the-art methods when tested using the Amazon Alexa ITN Challenge Dataset v3.

This paper demonstrates a Faber-Krahn type inequality for the first eigenvalue 
of the Hermite operator when subject to Robin boundary conditions, showing 
that the optimal configuration is a half-space, and investigates the conditions 
under which equality occurs.

Deep neural networks, though highly effective, are difficult to interpret, making them unsuitable for critical applications like medical imaging. Their reliability is compromised by the absence of formal guarantees, particularly when dealing with minor variations such as noise or alterations. To address this, a new approach is introduced that leverages optimal transport theory to create a specialized metric better suited for analyzing medical image data. This metric, known as OT, is then integrated into an iterative process designed to find the nearest input within an OT sphere, known IS^2, that can be classified by a deep neural network. By doing so, IS^2 is capable of accurately identifying medical images while remaining within the constraints of optimal transport. The optimal transport problem is solved through a simplified approach that uses a simplified and smoothed version of the original model, known sCP, and is accelerated using an adapted version of the Altland-Kiraly algorithm. The accelerated method is then used to establish an OT sphere around deep neural networks, specifically for the task of identifying renal pathology within medical images.

Despite extensive research on non-Hermitian topological systems, the effect of correlations has received relatively less attention. In a one-dimensional system with non-Hermitian dissipation, we discover that dissipation-related correlations significantly impact the topological classification, a phenomenon that can be further illustrated through the examination of an dissipative version of the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. By applying a modified version of the many-body Green's function in the context of the stochastic Schrödinger equation, we establish that the bulk-edge breakdown occurs only when correlations are present, a finding that is corroborated by the dissipative Zak phase. These results highlight the profound influence of dissipation-induced correlations on non-Hermitian topological systems.

Our current research builds upon our earlier findings that human voice conversion models have struggled to create a perception of warmth. To address this, we aim to investigate the characteristics of warmth in voice conversion by exploring the transfer of warmth from female to male voices. Through the use of a dataset and a prediction model, we will examine the role that various acoustic features play in warmth perception and test a theory that proposed minimal representation of the fundamental frequency band to achieve warmth.

A radiative seesaw model featuring light fermionic dark matter that acquires mass at one-loop level is presented. It naturally emerges from the $SU(2)_L \times SU(2)_R \times U(1)_{(L-R)}$ gauge symmetry breaking to $SU(2)_L \times U(1)_Y$, which breaks down to electromagnetic gauge symmetry. With the top quark mass reaching 173 GeV due to the radiative electroweak symmetry breaking, dark matter is found to have a mass ranging from a few hundred GeV to a few TeV. Radiative neutrino mass generation is found to be compatible with the dark matter relic density observed in the universe. Moreover, this model leaves an identifiable signature on the missing transverse energy plus jet or hadron jet searches at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC).

Building on the work of Bastin and Tannhauser, we introduced a theoretical extension to the Bohr-Mottelson model, incorporating a minimal length concept. Our research demonstrated that this minimal length idea arises naturally within the framework of quantum mechanics when applied to nuclear structure. We calculated the inertia parameters and potential energy for an oblate quadrupole nucleus as a function of the minimal length parameter, utilizing the Hill-Wheeler Gaussian approximation for the inertia parameters and Talmi coefficients for the potential energy. Our findings revealed that the minimal length parameter had little effect on the inertia parameters but significantly impacted the potential energy and, consequently, the collective Hamiltonian and low-lying energy spectra of the lowest 0_2^+ + 2_1^+ within the K=0 band of the prolate deformed nuclei 164,166,170,174,178,180,182,184,186,188,190,192,194,196,208,208,210,228,228,232,232,234,234,236,236,238,238,240,240,242,242,244,244,24

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained attention due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. Researchers have made efforts to construct GCMs of various lengths but many unresolved issues persist, particularly regarding GCMs of lengths that are multiples of 12. In this paper, a novel approach leveraging Golay complementary constellations will be introduced and utilized to develop GCMs of 12k length. The proposed method will demonstrate applicability by presenting GCMs of lengths 12 and 36.

Incorporating dimensionality reduction techniques and change detection methodologies into a unified framework is crucial in the analysis of multi-phase hyperspectral images. We address these requirements with a novel framework, the Feature Fusion Deep Convolutional Autoencoder (FFCDE), which utilizes a unified architecture to perform change detection across multiple phases of hyperspectral images automatically and in a supervised manner. By utilizing a hierarchical structure, the FFCDE reduces the complexity of raw images through Feature Representation (FR) blocks, effectively eliminating changes unrelated to spatial positioning and automatically learning changes in the images through Change Detection (CD) blocks. Furthermore, the FF is used to combine the newly learned features across phases, thereby reducing noise and boosting the accuracy of change detection processes. We evaluate the proposed FFCDE with multiple phases of Hyperspectral images and compare its performance with other state-of-the-art unsupervised and supervised change detection techniques. The results demonstrate that the FFCDE achieves superior performance in the unsupervised environment, highlighting its potential in the analysis of multi-phase hyperspectral images automatically.

A comprehensive study examines the connection between residual entropy and viscosity using an extensive, high-accuracy dataset for various molecular fluids. Comprising 380 datasets, the study includes data from multiple sources on diatomic and polyatomic systems over a broad pressure-temperature range. Results from polynomial fits reveal a striking, linear correlation between the system's residual entropy and the logarithmic viscosity in units of the SI bar and Pa s, respectively. The findings indicate that, when normalized, viscosity behaves as a linear function of residual entropy with an intrinsic slope. By comparing the data to a statistical thermodynamics model for simple fluids, we derive a state-independent linear relationship and a temperature-dependent slope with a temperature-like intercept for molecular fluids.

The possibility of an oscillating universe that periodically expands and contracts is considered as a form of cosmology to address the issues of flat entropy, the accelerated expansion, and the threat of a big rip. According to observations, our universe's expansion has indeed experienced transitions from slow to fast speeds and transitioned to an accelerated state. A new cosmological model based on a new dark energy equation of state is presented to address these features. The findings indicate that the proposed dark energy state remains stable. The possibility of a periodic cosmology remains plausible, though a definitive proof of such an oscillating universe remains elusive due to a lack of observational data during the early stages of our universe.

A new superdeterministic theory of quantum mechanics known as Invariant-set theory is being proposed. This idea requires correlations beyond what's allowed by the factorization of superdeterministic variables and exhibits contextuality when using context-dependent functions. Despite successfully accounting for quantum effects and making certain quantum predictions, questions remain about whether the theory accurately reflects reality independently of human choice. However, a closer examination reveals that earlier claims supporting the theory's validity are flawed when considering the structure of the theory's equations in relation to known issues with Bell correlations. Specifically, the way these issues arise is fundamentally different from what's claimed in the theory itself.

We examine Neural Networks (NNs) for keyword spotting tasks on devices such as smartphones and IoT sensors. To optimize these models for embedded systems, they must be compact, low-power consuming, and still maintain acceptable accuracy rates, necessitating the creation of highly efficient Convolutional NNs (CNNs). This paper presents MincNet, a compact and efficient CNN architecture, along with a highly optimized training technique. This study demonstrates the effectiveness of MincNet in performing KS tasks with exceptionally low power consumption and processing requirements, outperforming existing solutions. It achieves 91.1% accuracy while using just 0.042 milliwatts of power on a Raspberry Pi 3.

A key finding in this study is that when an additional variable in the direction perpendicular to the 2D space is integrated out of the 2D Dirac partition function in the presence of a gauge field, it yields a 2D Majorana fermion nonlinear sigma model where the target space includes a 2-form superfield and a B-field, with specific couplings dependent on the color of the integrated boson. This discovery enables us to identify certain aspects of the B-field couplings that remain unaffected by color, while the remaining aspects facilitate connections between the couplings, making the couplings' uniqueness not hold true when the color exceeds a certain value, specifically color > 2.

Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, particularly when observations must be fully reduced in complex data subsets. The current state of research lacks an appropriate framework for tackling this challenge, with existing algorithms requiring either exhaustive searches or risking suboptimal performance. The proposed research introduces an efficient method for sparsity exploration using mixed integer programming, applied initially to an exploratory study of the \emph{Adolescent Brain Cognitive} dataset, involving \emph{ABC}4 data, categorized variables, and binary outcomes. The outcome was the identification of a comprehensive yet easily interpretable model containing 11 variables, including 2 categorical variables, offering accurate predictions and retaining brain variables in final sparsity exploration outcomes, in contrast to continuous models with either \emph{LASSO} or \emph{Best Subset Selection}.

In recent years, the demands for higher security and reliability in embedded real-time systems have led to an increased need for virtualization. Currently, few embedded virtualization technologies meet these requirements for safety-critical applications. To address this need, we propose T-Visor, a real-time virtualization hypervisor for mixed-criticality embedded systems. It offers several key features that distinguish it from traditional virtualization solutions, including zero security violations to SIFAs, minimal power consumption, real-time scheduling, and support for live migration. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of T-Visor in providing robust security and real-time performance on ARM-based platforms.

When creating panoramic images, any initial misalignment of cameras can lead to inaccurate stitching due to off-center angles. Existing panoramic creation tools often require manual adjustment of camera angles, a labor-intensive process. Although automatic in-the-wild calibration has been addressed, it remains overlooked for panoramic settings. We delve into a novel problem of calibrating off-vertical panoramic cameras, and introduce Prismo, a comprehensive system for addressing this challenge. Prismo begins by collecting reference images to calibrate camera intrinsics, then uses these settings to off-level calibration using reference images or a demo interface. Finally, Prismo produces panoramic views incorporating the adjusted camera extrinsics. Through both real-world experiments and benchmark testing, Prismo demonstrates significant improvements in panoramic creation, surpassing approaches based on vertical camera assumptions and building upon prior extrinsic adjustments in panoramic settings.

When two coupled populations of oscillators have synchronized and asynchronous elements respectively, a chimeric state occurs. This phenomenon has primarily been studied in systems comprising Marquardt oscillators, which have type I nonlinearity. Our research focuses on the CHINOS population of oscillators with type II nonlinearity. We discovered that two different types of chimeras, known as in-phase and out-of-phase, can emerge when two coupled Marqusert population oscillators are connected through diffusive coupling. Our study also identified a phase transition between these two types of chimeric states and found that only one of these types is typically observed in experimental settings.

We examine if controllers obtained using model-based reinforcement learning, that are designed to be sample-efficient by learning a transition model of the environment, also excel in adaptability. Specifically, we investigate how these controllers compare to model-free controllers in their ability to transfer skills across similar but fundamentally different environments. Although controllers based on model-free methods typically fall short in their adaptability, often surpassing them requires fine-tuning the policy for each new environment. In contrast, our experiments reveal that model-based controllers not only outperform model-free ones in their sample-savings, but also do so naturally, without any adjustments.

We present a multi-layer quiver of infinite type, from which we derive a classification system for its slice algebras. This classification is demonstrated to have applications in converting the representation theory of each slice algebra to the more familiar representation theory of a finite dimensional algebra. Additionally, the concept is applied to establish a connection between the representation categories of two different infinite type algebras, specifically the Leavitt path algebra for the loop with an edge intersection and the Leavitt path algebra for the regular tame category.

Research in holographic field theories has shown that the reflection coefficient approaches 1 for certain states, but previous models based on random tensor networks failed to exhibit this behavior due to the lack of non-trivial correlations. Our research examines under what conditions random tensor networks display non-classical behavior similar to complex field theories. We discover that incorporating the subtleties of reduced density matrices and the cross-entropy term reveals an underlying pattern in the network's correlations that generates the desired behavior. Crucially, our findings indicate that only correlations associated with the cross-entropy contribute to the network's ability to mimic reflection coefficient-driven phenomena like the non-trivial mutual information and the first and second order phase transitions observed in ground states.

The rapid increase in the number of available datasets has led to a surge in research focused on uncovering patterns within complex, high-dimensional data. A key objective is to pinpoint persistent patterns, as they offer valuable insights into an underlying system. In this study, we introduce a method for identifying patterns that endure over time. Our approach reveals an intriguing connection between the rate at which a system's entropy increases and the longevity of these patterns. Notably, our findings indicate that even short-lived patterns can be reliably retrieved when the system's size becomes sufficiently large and that multiple significant patterns can emerge simultaneously. To further validate our method, we have successfully applied it to analyze the dynamics of systems governed by diverse nonlinear ordinary differential equations.

We investigate the characteristics of a dynamical system on a two-dimensional surface, specifically focusing on how its boundary impacts the formation of specific types of chaotic orbits. By considering the Hamiltonian version of the Gaussian free field on the upper half plane, we derive the spectral parameter scaling laws for unique "dragonfly" orbits that occur when there are obstacles at specific points.

The fundamental principle of the double copy connects gauge theory and gravity, but its underpinning principles remain unclear, so researchers use the effective field theory framework to gain a deeper understanding. When considering the high-energy behavior of interactions, specific patterns in gauge theory and gravity scatter amplitudes emerge, allowing for a precise comparison. A particular mathematical model can effectively capture the relationship between gauge theory and gravity amplitudes at high energies, even when considering interactions with light particles, as demonstrated in this study. Using the eikonal model to describe the phase shift obtained from these amplitudes, researchers derived the large-energy behavior of scattering events involving external particles in the gravity theory and matched it with predictions from the gauge theory side. A newly developed formula for the gauge theory side outperforms older models, accurately predicting scattering events in the gravitational regime.

We have investigated how certain properties related to partitions of a fixed integer n compare when part of the parts are dock hooks. Specifically, the mean and variance were studied for parts divisible by a preselected integer t. Our analysis showed that as n increases, the normalized statistics for these parts converge to a normal distribution. Additionally, some previously documented results were generalized, including the mean and variance for all dock hooks across all partitions of n, which were first documented in Dousse (2019).

Quantum particles experiencing tunneling can be studied through various theoretical models, each leading to differing conclusions about tunneling time. Despite using different approaches, researchers have been unable to reach a consensus on whether tunneling time is a fixed constant, varies with energy levels, or even exists in the first place. In an attempt to resolve this issue experimentally, a study is proposed that involves observing the changes in the frequency of Larmor precession when a spin-1/2 particle tunnels through a barrier in the presence of an electromagnetic field. The goal is to determine tunneling time by analyzing the variations in the particle's energy as it undergoes Larmor precession. This can be achieved by comparing the time spent in the classically accessible region to that spent in the tunneling period using energy conservation principles applied to both scenarios.

This research investigates the leading twist distribution amplitudes of P-wave non-relativistic mesons, demonstrating that at a leading order approximation, these amplitudes can be represented by a single, universal function, irrespective of specific meson types. As an example, the amplitudes for P-wave charmonia mesons are studied, utilizing QCD sum rules to establish a model for the universal function specific to this meson type. Moreover, the research establishes connections between the moments of the universal function and the matrix elements controlling non-relativistic corrections in P-wave charmonia amplitudes. Our findings reveal that the characteristic magnitude of these relativistic corrections amounts to approximately thirty percent.

Research in nonlinear quantum mechanics may hold potential for quantum information processing and interferometry advancement.  We suggest examining nonlinearities that arise due to interactions between distinct, non-entangled qubits.  We've discovered that this interaction-based 'classical-like' nonlinearity doesn't have any byproduct effects, thus making it possible to analyze them rigorously using the framework of unitary, trace-preserving qubit evolutions.  We've examined various properties of these unitary evolution operators and found that they often exhibit ambiguities when applied to states composed of multiple copies.  We've demonstrated that, despite exhibiting local separability, these evolution operators typically fail to maintain contextuality and non-Bellian properties, unlike their single-copy counterpart.

The extended BMS algebra plays a crucial role in understanding quantum gravity's S-matrix. It emerges as the asymptotic symmetry algebra of massless gravity in four-dimensional flat space, fully capturing black hole and graviton observations. In this work, the extended BMS algebra is represented as the central extension of the remarkable infinite-dimensional algebra known as the Witt bigrading of bimodules. It has an equivalent form through the semidirect sum of the central extension of the Witt algebra with two abelian algebras. A novel cohomology method has been developed to achieve this representation, simplifying the previously complex computation by reducing the involved orders and revealing the infinite-order central extensions' relationships.

Learning with an ever-growing number of categories poses significant challenges. The task becomes particularly demanding when models need to learn online and from examples seen just once. The issue of severe class imbalance also complicates learning processes. Our research introduces a novel approach that tackles these issues by employing a mixture of experts model, where each expert specializes in a particular category, coupled with a soft allocation mechanism that allows multiple experts to contribute equally to the initial learning phase. The proposed method yields state-of-the-art results on established benchmarks, outperforming existing techniques in scenarios with larger numbers of categories.
In metric geometry and general relativity, specifically Einstein's vacuum equations, generalized complex structures and Galilean Cartan structures play pivotal roles.

In this study, several new families of permutation polynomials on the finite field with $q^3$ elements are introduced and proven. These families are constructed using a variety of methods, including inverse, semi-linear, almost linear, and reciprocal mappings. Additionally, a few theorems on the inversion in $\mathbb{F}_{q^3}$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$ and $\mathbb{Z}_p$ are discovered and applied to generate novel families of permutation polynomials.

Approximately 1.5 billion individuals worldwide are affected by intestinal parasitic infections, which pose significant health risks to both developing and developed nations by triggering gastrointestinal inflammation and systemic disorders. Infected pets also contribute substantially to the spread of these parasites. The cost of eliminating parasites from human populations is exorbitant, necessitating the development of cost-effective diagnostic tools. While non-invasive detection methods are crucial for low-income areas, existing non-stool-based diagnostics are scarce. Our study aims to explore the potential of using non-human variables, such as dog owner characteristics and environmental factors, to predict human falcon infections using machine learning techniques. Our findings demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in accurately forecasting human parasitic infections, which may facilitate innovative cost-efficient diagnostic methods for areas lacking proper healthcare infrastructure.

This work introduces a novel framework for analyzing and solving stochastic differential investment and reinsurance games that take into account both proportional and limited loss reinsurance contracts. A division into subcases is made, namely games with two and three players. Our analysis reveals that all two-player games and three-player games with one player offering reinsurance can be reduced to solving a single nonlinear partial differential equation (PDE). A novel approach is introduced to solve these nonlinear PDEs. Our findings are validated with a variety of numerical examples.

This research presents a novel Proportional-Integral-Derivative-Accelerated (PIDA) control strategy, integrating a derivative filter, to enhance quadcopter stability in chaotic and unpredictable flight conditions. The implementation of MATLAB proves effective in conjunction with the OpenCV-J Java/C++ library to process images captured by a webcam. This approach enables the tracking of a specific point on the quadcopter, thereby facilitating rotation control in three dimensions. The proposed PIDA controller, in conjunction with visual feedback, has been successfully implemented in quadcopter flight and has demonstrated significant improvement in tracking accuracy and mitigation of perturbations, outperforming the traditional Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) controller, especially in the presence of disturbances.

study.
